When cinema visionary Mooky Greidinger makes a move, the industry pays attention. This is the man who took a small family-owned chain in Israel, merged it with Cineworld and helped build the world’s second-largest cinema group.

So when the news hit last week that Greidinger is back in the UK, having acquired Showcase’s 16-strong UK circuit and signed a major deal with Imax to roll out laser systems at 12 of its sites, the sector took notice.

It’s a big, bold move. But it’s also highly significant for the message it sends out: cinemas are still big business, and they have a big future.

UK cinemas: From lockdown to new heights

Six years ago the sector was singing a very different tune. Lockdowns were devastating. UK attendance in 2020 was down 75 per cent on the previous year, leaving entertainment groups here and around the world needing huge government subsidies just to keep going.

But keep going they did, and as 2026 draws to a close, there are clear signs even beyond the Showcase deal that the sector is not just back but reaching new heights: innovating, transforming, developing new formats and ideas. It’s been a decade of challenge and change. And cinemas have listened.

Even so, in 2026, issues remain. Change is still happening. Struggling sites are closing down. Attendance and sales figures are still in flux.

Odeon and the blockbuster summer

A year ago Odeon reported a sharp drop in attendance but a big increase in box office revenue, thanks to higher ticket prices. We await Odeon’s full-year 2026 results, but we know that the summer was a golden one for the group. With a little help no doubt from Christopher Nolan blockbuster The Odyssey, Odeon’s summer attendance was 33 per cent up on 2025 – its highest figures since before Covid.

In fact the whole sector breathed a sigh of relief this blockbuster summer, thanks to The Odyssey and just behind that Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The net result: admissions in August 2026 passed 17m, an increase of 56 per cent on the same month in 2025. Since Covid, only the Barbenheimer phenomenon of July 2023 has drawn more people through the doors in a single month.

Showcase Cinemas and Imax: The lesson for Vue and its rivals

Just the news that UK group Vue needed to hear, if rumours of a stock market float are to be believed. But it takes more than a few big summer blockbusters for that kind of move. Vue has wisely invested big across its portfolio, with refurbs such as the transformation of its Finchley Road site in London, completed in September 2026.

If the Vue float rumour is the teaser for a future, rejuvenated cinema business, Mooky Greidinger’s Showcase and Imax deal is the all-star cast and the after-party combined. And it is a lesson: if cinemas are going to thrive in the modern era, they need the latest tech, and the best possible screens. And that means big bucks going in.

Take note. Because without major investment and smart portfolio management, all the blockbusters Hollywood can make won’t be enough. Leisure habits are changing. Cinemas need to offer more than just popcorn and a screen – Imax 4K laser screens are just one example – to get customers off their sofas.

That means expanding and diversifying your offer to customers. Transforming places and properties. Creating truly mixed-use leisure spaces, with enough excitement to entice the whole family.

The Light Banbury: Cinema as a leisure destination

Everywhere you look there are inspiring examples. To call The Light in Banbury a cinema would be like calling Oppenheimer a story about science. The multi-use venue, opened in 2022, is a complex of bars, food options, a climbing wall, mini golf, karaoke booths, darts, bowling, soft play, and yes, a cinema.

Opening when it did, after so much turmoil, might not have been possible had The Light been a cinema alone. But with so much to offer so many ages and group dynamics, it goes far beyond that. And it may just be the future of the mainstream cinema sector.

There are groups investing in their existing estates. There are groups expanding. Take the steady growth of Nottingham-based indie chain Savoy, mainly through acquisitions, taking the group’s portfolio to nine sites. Or the continued expansion of Everyman, notably in Elephant & Castle, where a future five-screen cinema will be one of the company’s biggest in London. And there are those inspiring local stories, such as the news that a new 10,000 square foot three-screen cinema is heading to the North Yorkshire city of Ripon.

Which cuts to the core of why cinemas matter, and mean so much to people and places.

The future of the cinema industry

It’s been a testing decade for cinemas. But there are signs like these everywhere now, not just of a renewal, but a renaissance in real-life experiences. Retail and leisure spaces aren’t just reviving. They’re being reborn, out of necessity. And we say now it’s cinema’s turn.

The message of the last 10 years wasn’t that cinema’s days are over. Far from it. The message was that people need more than just a movie to get them out of the house. So, the smart companies have given them more: games, sports, entertainment, food and film; rich, exciting places, unique to their towns and high streets.

These visionaries are creating places greater than the sum of their parts. They are writing the future of leisure and entertainment, and a tantalising sequel in the neverending story of the silver screen.

articles.title: National Lottery’s slow death is squeezing life out of British sport
articles.summary:
Britain’s Olympic sports are battling rising costs while their National Lottery funding flatlines, warns Ed Warner.

Is my door in the draw? I’ve no idea. How does the Postcode Lottery work? If my neighbour buys a winning ticket does our shared postcode entitle me to a share of the spoils? And what are her chances of success? 

What it appears to this avid Planet Rock listener is that there are only two lotteries in the market. The Postcode one and another offering a chance to win hundreds of thousands of pounds if I text ROCK to 64100 and stand by to answer my phone on a Friday afternoon. National Lottery, where art thou?

The grand dame of British lotteries is in the news once again this week. The business pages report that the National Lottery’s operator Allwyn has postponed a dual listing for its shares. You can currently find them on the Athens Stock Exchange, down in value by a third since they first listed on 1 April this year by way of a merger with a Greek lottery company. 

Cue regurgitated stories of the controversial franchise war with incumbent operator Camelot that Allwyn won in 2022, and the company’s failure to meet revenue targets in its nearly three years of operating the Lottery so far.

This all matters for British sport because the nation’s Olympic and Paralympic programmes are heavily dependent on distributions from the “good causes” pot created by Lottery ticket sales, as are many grassroots sporting organisations. The same is true, of course, of a swathe of bodies across other sectors deemed integral to the nation’s identity and wellbeing, especially the arts.

Forget for now Allwyn’s bid boast that it would double the sums flowing to good causes – after all, bid promises in any industry must always be taken with a fistful of salt. Instead focus on the raw numbers. The latest data from the Gambling Commission shows an annual £1.6bn generated for good causes by the Lottery. However, the most recent three-month numbers reveal a 16 per cent year-on-year decline.

The current economic climate is clearly a challenge that any lottery operator would struggle to overcome. Inflation is eating into household incomes. 

It would be unrealistic to expect this squeeze to trigger a spike in sales of a product that offers a very long-odds possibility of winning a life-changing sum, or indeed of scratchcards that might bring a far smaller injection of cash. [Park at this point the debate about the morality of state-endorsed gambling products and their impact on some of the more economically vulnerable members of the population].

For recipients of National Lottery funding – and I write as one, being chair of GB Wheelchair Rugby – the impact of economic conditions is brutal. 

Our costs are inflating while the funding we receive from the Lottery via the state’s agencies, UK Sport and Sport England, flatlines. In real terms, this funding income is down by more than a fifth over the past six years. The same is true for most other governing bodies.

My fear is that the National Lottery is in irreversible decline, its competitors too numerous, its products out-dated and incapable of reinvention radical enough to reverse the venture’s tide, and any psychological link between ticket buying and benefit to good causes lost in the mists of time, never to be recovered.

Remember the football pools? A staple of my youth, watching my father tick off the score draws on his coupon during the 5pm announcement of Saturday’s results. They still exist, it appears, cunningly branded The Football Pools. The Telegraph recently cited experts believing that fewer than 200,000 people now play each month, a fraction of the peak of 14m in the mid 80s.

For the nation’s dreamers, from 19 November 1994 footy results on the radio made way for big-money balls on prime time Saturday evening BBC1, Noel Edmonds and all that. Not quite a “stop the nation” moment each week, but not far off. Seems an age ago now. The last live draw on the Beeb was 10 years ago next month.

The National Lottery may prove to have a long half-life, but its decay over time seems inevitable, to be eaten away by changes in behaviour of consumers lured by new and more agile competitors. 

The blurring of identities between lotteries and gambling can only be steepening the National Lottery’s decline. How to hold onto a share of a consumer’s mind (or wallet) when they are being bombarded by ads for sports betting and online gaming?

Meantime, lottery-funded British sports need to plot paths to greater financial independence. Politicians, too, would do well to reflect on the importance of sport to the nation and debate ways beyond the Lottery in which they can assist in securing its healthy future – both on the field of play and at the bank.

Rubber tickets

I’ve been positively surprised by the level of engagement – my own included – with rugby’s new Nations Championship format that has provided some coherence to the annual string of one-off contests in both hemispheres. I do, though, wonder whether a three-day, six-match finals weekend at a single venue is quite what teams and fans crave.

Better surely to have a pair of matches on a single day to rank the top four nations. Let the others have a weekend off. Do fans really care sufficiently about lesser rankings, or are these other games essentially dead rubbers? Ticket sales might give us the answer.

A sinister turn of events

A friend departing LGW in search of Moroccan winter sun bumped into an organiser of the World Association of Left Handed Golfers’ 30th World Championship, which is currently underway in Marrakech. 

Who knew? Good luck to all those involved. Are there any equivalent events in other sports, I wonder? Can’t find any on a quick Google search.

Ed Warner is chair of Sussex Cricket and GB Wheelchair Rugby and writes his sport column at sportinc.substack.com

articles.title: Kevin the Carrot’s future in doubt: Christmas adverts 2026 reviewed, part two
articles.summary:
It feels a bit more Christmassy now, doesn’t it? It’s bloody cold, and it really feels like we’re cruising into the season to be jolly. No doubt about it. The lights are everywhere. Baileys is 10 quid on discount. Noel, my PR guy, has finally worked out which of his 39 Christmas jumpers he’s going to wear. And I’ve already rather biliously eaten my own body weight of ‘party nibbles’.

This is part two of the Christmas advert review bit. If you missed part one, this year, rather than just me wanging on, I’m comparing what we, in the adland bubble, think about the work (ads to you), to what you think. Are we on the money… or are we just talking to ourselves, which has been known to happen? We kicked off with John Lewis, M&S and Tesco last week, of which you were loving M&S a lot more than John Lewis. A new king is born. How appropriate.

Waitrose Christmas advert 2026: The Perfect Gift 2 goes primetime

Waitrose is another favourite. With everyone actually. Last year ITV didn’t run The Perfect Gift in an ad break. It commissioned it into the schedule and premiered it at 8pm across three channels, like a proper programme. This year, the sequel got the same treatment, six minutes of primetime ITV right before Emmerdale. It got a bit of flak for being too long, but the argument for that is that it didn’t interrupt the entertainment… it was the entertainment. The 30- and 60-second trailers are the ads, and they do the selling. System1 (a measurement platform) sees it differently. It tested the full six minutes the way it tests any commercial and gave it 5.6 stars, down on the original’s 5.9. But remember. If you sit a panel down in front of a six-minute film and judge it like a 30-second ad it was always going to lose a few points on length. It still posted one of the strongest Spike Ratings of the year, which tells you people walked away wanting to shop at Waitrose. The real winner is Joe Wilkinson. Who 20 years ago, before he was a comedian, worked for me in an ad agency. And this year… he gets Keira. From behind the cameras to the front…

Play Video

Morrisons Christmas advert 2026: Goldilocks gets the laughs

Whereas Waitrose is long and well branded, Morrisons’ ‘Made just right’ is only (!!) 90 seconds, and is wonderfully charming but less tied to the brand. We’ve got a modern take on Goldilocks, who rocks up for Christmas dinner on the arm of the younger bear. There are some lovely filmic touches, not least the bear scoring the salmon prior to roasting with its claws rather than a knife. System1 has it joint first with Saino’s on 5.9. You guys apparently thought it was the funniest ad of the year so far, with 45 per cent saying it made you laugh… But it’s only fifth on your league table. You’re a tough crowd. Doesn’t a laugh count for anything at Christmas?

Play Video

Aldi Christmas advert 2026: Kevin the Carrot turns 10

So moving along the high street we stumble into Aldi. By now Kevin the Carrot is a seasonal familiar – like indigestion or the family argument – but all of us love him. Kevin is 10 years old (can you believe it) but System1 gives it a perfect score for the fourth time in five years. Marketing Week scores it top for empathy and making you feel good about the brand. That’s pretty damn good for a root vegetable. You? You rank it joint second with Waitrose… a massive 73 per cent of you want Kevin back next year. And there. My friends. Is the problem. Even though we all love him… Aldi has just changed agencies. Oh my word. The injustice!! Will the new agency can the carrot? The thing with your creative type is that when given the choice between carrying on with something someone else dreamed up, or creating their own work… the latter wins every time. So, maybe the new year will be a bit dicey for the carrot? All of us will have to wait till next Christmas to find out. It really is a brutal business…

Play Video

The verdict: Waitrose wins on love, Morrisons on laughs

Anyway. That’s your lot. A beef Wellington, three bears and a carrot on death row carried Christmas again. Time to pour yourself a massive sherry and put the ‘out of office’ on. For me Waitrose wins on love but Morrisons wins on laughs. Merry Christmas.

articles.title: Blame Labour and the Tories for your gas bill going up by £443
articles.summary:
The Tories started the net zero madness and Labour promised green energy would be cheaper. Reform will ditch green levies and arbitrary targets and cut your bills, says Richard Tice

Cast your minds back to the 2024 general election. Labour’s eco-zealot energy spokesman Ed Miliband stood before the British public and with customary ill-deserved confidence announced that rushing headlong into intermittent green energy would usher in an era of cheap, abundant, home-grown power.

Vote for us, proclaimed Red Ed, and we will cut your energy bills by £300.

Fast forward nearly three years and the exact opposite has turned out to be true. Ofgem’s announcement that it will be raising the energy price cap by 26 per cent in January means the average household bill will climb by £443 a year.

With families already struggling with food prices and never ending tax rises there was a never good time to face an energy price hike.

But for it to come just after Christmas, with the dreaded arrival of holiday credit card statements, depleted savings and bank accounts stretched thin by gifts and travel, it is an especially cruel blow.

Far from reducing our energy bills, under Labour they will have now risen in total by £883. Mr Miliband and his colleagues should frankly hang their heads in shame.

Needless to say, the government is already reaching for the same tired excuses.

They point to global gas markets and instability in the Middle East. While Nobody denies that the world is an uncertain place, that is precisely why any serious government would maximise Britain’s own domestic energy resources.

Instead, consecutive Conservative and Labour governments have treated our North Sea oil and gas treasure like an enemy.

Even though Britain sits on hundreds of millions of barrels of oil and vast reserves of natural gas in fields like Rosebank, ministers have preferred to block domestic extraction, leaving us dangerously exposed to volatile international imports.

Shipping liquefied natural gas across the globe at premium prices while leaving British resources locked beneath the seabed is economic self-harm on an industrial scale. Worse still, importing energy from abroad actually generates higher global emissions than producing it right here at home.

Reform will end the madness

Meanwhile, hidden beneath every single gas and electricity bill are the punishing green levies designed to bankroll Westminster’s net zero obsession, leaving households and businesses forced to pay some of the highest industrial and domestic electricity prices in the developed world. Just remember, those levies don’t just affect your energy bill. They are baked into the price of every loaf of bread and every pint of milk on our high streets.

The government’s temporary sticking-plaster handouts – a £100 payment here, a six-month pause on electricity VAT there – do nothing to fix a fundamentally broken system. Because in April, bills are expected to rise even further. We simply cannot go on like this.

Reform UK will end this madness.

We will scrap net zero targets, abolish the punitive green levies and permanently remove VAT from both domestic gas and electricity.

We would fast-track North Sea licences, unlock fields like Rosebank, and restore genuine British energy security so that our power supply is reliable, affordable, and under our own control.

Because make no mistake, net zero is without question the most naive, reckless and ill-thought through policy the political establishment has unleashed on the public in my lifetime.

And when you think of some of the bone-headed decisions made by the main political parties over two decades, from Hs2 to their farcical handling of the pandemic, that really is saying something.

It is nothing more than an arbitrary target pursued by vainglorious politicians without any consideration whatsoever of the financial consequences.

And in the process of doing so, they have made our bills higher, left our homes colder and our business and industries considerably weaker.

So when that eye-watering bill drops onto your doormat in the New Year just remember it’s the Tories and Labour who are to blame.

Richard Tice is business, trade and energy spokesman for Reform UK

articles.title: The Capitalist: How to enter a party in style? Sled down the stairs like Jeremy Goring
articles.summary:
A royal visit to Winter Wonderland, tiny ponies at The Goring and the battle of the Christmas trees; catch up on the latest gossip in this week’s The Capitalist

PARTIES, PRINCES AND PONIES

It may not be December yet but London is in full Christmas party swing, and The Capitalist is absolutely exhausted. 

First, Winter Wonderland, which every year opens its fake-snow topped gates to press for a VIP preview night, inclusive of all rides, attractions and a fair few pretzels. The Capitalist most enjoys not having to go with the rest of London’s rabble though, as do, apparently, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who were spotted enjoying a ride on the dodgems and a go on the hook-a-duck with their children Archie and Lillibet. 

Indeed, The Capitalist was wondering why so many delightful children in £300 coats were getting in their way in the wacky house; turns out the night is also open to the general public (deep breaths) as a charity night, with fees from the £120 tickets (and £80 for their little chiddlers) all going towards The Royal Parks. 

If you prefer your slides inside lavish hotels though, head to The Goring, where chief executive Jeremy Goring entered his Christmas party sledding down the stairs pursued by robbers. The entrance, a tribute to Home Alone, was just a taste of the zaniness that characterises the annual knees up, famously attended each year also by tiny Shetland pony Teddy for guests to pose with under the Christmas tree. The Capitalist was reluctant to leave at midnight carriages, though rumour was Robert de Niro was staying upstairs in the penthouse, and presumably needed some shuteye.

BACK IN QUIZNESS

Which colourful billionaire made a cameo as himself in the Simpsons in 2015? That is just one of the questions that perplexed free market fans at a quiz to bid farewell to Robert Colvile as director of the Centre for Policy Studies, Margaret Thatcher’s think tank. City AM‘s ‘Quizness with Personality’ team put in a solid performance, beating a team from a rival media organisation but losing out in the politics-heavy contest to a team called ‘Breaking Spads’. 

Our own Alys Denby did come close to winning the bonus prize, a bottle of wine worth £700 donated by CPS chair and NEX founder Michael Spencer – like the Rachel Reeves of this particular competition she was the only woman in the final – but also like Rachel Reeves she was ousted by an opponent with a dubious mandate (the victor was rumoured to have cheated). 

And if you’re wondering what’s the answer to the most diabolical picture round in Westminster, it’s Elon Musk.

BATTLE OF THE CHRISTMAS TREES

The Ned’s stylist spent eight hours making each and every bow on their spectacular Christmas tree this year, which you can see above, as revealed exclusively by City AM. Across town, a luxury arms race to install the biggest and best fir has begun. At Claridge’s, Father Christmas himself greeted The Capitalist this Wednesday, seated within his treehouse beneath Dame Anya Hindmarch’s tree, which spirals up beyond the lobby towards the first floor bedrooms.

For us, Santa had just one question: “You had an indiscretion this September, didn’t you?” We promised him we’d been well behaved – as had he, evidently: the hotel purposefully hired an in-shape Santa this year, to blow apart the notion he needs to oversized. With all the mince pies doing the rounds in the foyer, though, one must wonder whether Mr Claws’ present to himself is in GLP-1 form. But how does Santa process all those letters? “Claude, Chat GPT, we use all of them,” the exasperated former letter writer said.

THE LONDON MUSEUM PROVES… INTERESTING

Could the new London Museum be too woke even for the Guardian? The paper’s critic joined The Telegraph in penning an unfavourable review, featuring a devastating line on museum management’s use of Orwellian language: “Displays have nonsensical themes: “London as Ritual”, “London as Stage”, “London as Sunrise”. One wall text begins: “London is a city of people.” Read that twice. What is this? Cunk on London?”

articles.title: The 13 best City of London restaurants, from a Michelin-starred hideaway to a former bear pit
articles.summary:
These are the City of London restaurants our Toast the City writers rate most, from Michelin-starred tasting menus to Victorian institutions and bold new openings, with each pick taken from our original reviews and features.

Fine dining restaurants in the City of London

Restaurant St Barts

St Barts is a Michelin-starred restaurant that only uses British ingredients in its tasting menus. Crowe, who co-founded St Barts in 2022 with Luke Wasserman and Toby Neill, has built a restaurant around his producers. Before Barts, the trio owned Nest in Shoreditch, which this summer was transformed into the much-lauded and much-Instagrammed British bistro Tavern. But St Barts is where Crowe’s dogged devotion to homegrown suppliers pushes him to put out a seriously unique menu. 

Read the full piece

Galvin La Chapelle

Amid the change, Galvin La Chapelle – a stand-out Square Mile building that quite literally feels like a chapel – is a resilient cornerstone of the Square Mile. It’s the sort of place that feels as if it can stop time briefly when you go in for a meal. Half a million was spent on a post-pandemic refurbishment to lighten the furnishings and make the place feel ever so slightly more casual, but it still retains its aura of a destination restaurant, the type of place that totally consumes you for a few hours. “We don’t have a ‘no phones’ policy but rarely do people use phones in the restaurant,” says Chris. “They engage with their friends, which is special.”

Read the full piece

Angler

The best ingenuity remains on the plate. Angler specialises, as you’d hope, in the food of the sea. I went for the eight-course tasting menu, but there is a four-course option and an a la carte menu. Here, again, contemporary ideas clash with tradition: there is great care to explain every dish, but no-one’s talking your ear off. Service is friendly, not stifling. Plates are full up with food and not so artfully designed that you need to pop to McDonald’s after.

Read the full piece

Luna Omakase

But located down a black stone corridor lies somewhere close to the antithesis of all this noise and colour: a calm, thoughtful space somewhere between a private dining room and a restaurant-within-a-restaurant. Luna Omakase is, as the name suggests, a Japanese omakase joint, a concept now fairly well established in London, where a theatrical and often outré tasting menu is prepared and served from behind a counter.

Read the full piece

Classic City of London restaurants

Sweetings

The original interior remains: acres of dark wood, an imposing bar with stools at which diners can perch if they choose, and tables for the more conventional and milquetoast clientele. For the experience alone, it’s worth ordering Black Velvet to drink: although the 50/50 mixture of Guinness and champagne was first served in Brooks’s Club in St James’s in 1861 to mark the sudden death of Prince Albert, Sweetings has leaned heavily into its Victorian associations, serving it in silver tankards for that elusive and very British combination of prosperous high living and boorishness.

Read the full piece

Liverpool Street Chop House

More than anywhere else on Evolv’s books, Chop House is a paean to meat. After I’m seated, a waiter rumbles over with a trolley filled with the cuts of the day, spinning it around like a magician showing you the sides of his box before he chops his assistant in half. Here’s the fillet, here’s the intimidating-looking, bone-in ribeye, here are the chops. Meat, meat, meat, meat, meat.

Read the full piece

Bob Bob Ricard City

The resulting restaurant in the Cheesegrater is like passing through a hall of mirrors into a giant pinball machine. It gives you the feeling that if it were tipped on its side or upside-down, Inception-style, it would look exactly the same. It’s like looking at an optical illusion: one minute it’s a pastiche of a 1950s diner, the next it’s the cabin of a private jet, then a latter-day Damien Hirst installation. It’s brilliant and bonkers and we at City AM are huge fans.

Read the full piece

High Timber

What is it? Despite being one of the City’s most established restaurants (it’s 17 years old and I first wrote about it 15 years ago), you’d be forgiven for overlooking this little gem nestled on the North Bank, not least because you have to navigate the impenetrable Upper Thames Street to get to it. Once you make it there, however, you’re greeted by surely the finest river view in all of London, with Southwark Bridge to your left, Millennium Bridge to your right and Shakespeare’s Globe and the Tate Modern straight ahead.

Read the full piece

The best new and international restaurants in the Square Mile

Ibai

If you have already heard about Ibai, I’ll wager it had something to do with the Galician Blond steak, cut from cattle reared for no less than 14 years by a bloke called Xose Portas (the Basque folk do love an ‘X’) on his farm in Pontevedra. These animals have been around long enough to develop a mature, quite chewy marbling and a thick wedge of fat. This isn’t melt-in-your-mouth wagyu, rather a deep, rich slab of meat that requires thoughtful – nay, mindful – chewing. 

Read the full piece

Leydi at Hyde London City

Leydi by chef Selin Kiazim is bringing incredible modern Turkish flavours to the Square Mile, from the chef formerly of the much-loved institution Oklava.

Read the full piece

Campanelle

Campanelle is one of our favourite new Square Mile restaurants, a vast Italian dining room set inside the beautifully restored London Shipping Exchange on Billiter Street. Created by restaurateur Ninai Zarach, the all-day venue is an excellent showcase for grand City architecture.

Read the full piece

Brigadiers

Brigadiers is a strange proposition, a sports bar-cum-Indian barbecue inspired by the wood panelled army bars of the sub-continent but housed in the polished surrounds of Bloomberg Arcade. 

Read the full piece

Libertine at the Royal Exchange

The newly-opened Libertine restaurant at the Royal Exchange is allegedly where bears were kept. I was skeptical until the lady behind the bar told me the whole story, then a waiter corroborated it, and then so did the manager.

Read the full piece

articles.title: City pay war heats up as bonus payout season arrives for US law firms
articles.summary:
Junior lawyers at US law firms across the City are gearing up to pocket their bonus payouts, driving up the already fierce pay-war in the industry.

The scale serves as a benchmark for major law firms to set associate pay, which follow suit when Cravath shares its compensation figures for the year.

Many US law firms operate under the so-called Cravath Scale, named after the law firm which historically set it, Cravath, Swaine & Moore, a transparent, associate pay scale of compensation anchored to post-qualification experience. It ensures that associates have a clear understanding of what their year-end bonus will be.

Cravath announced on 17 November it is hiking pay for the firm’s associates in both the US and London, with base pay now ranging from $235,000 for its class of 2026 associates to $440,000 for those from 2019 and above from 1 January 2027.

The move then prompted ​Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton, both of which have a large presence in the City as well as the US, ⁠to follow Cravath’s lead, according to Reuters.

Post-merger communication issues

On Tuesday, Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, the firm which made history in July when it merged with the oldest legal practice on Wall Street, marking the largest transatlantic legal merger on record, moved to adopt the salary scale, as reported by Non-Billable.

The firm is set to increase base pay to $235,000 for associates in the class of 2026, rising to $455,000 for the more senior associates.

Base salaries for legacy Cadwaladar associates in London will run from £176,250 for first-year associates to £341,250 for seniors – £31,250 above the £145,000 rate for newly qualified lawyers in London, announced by the firm in June pre-merger.

Ria Karnik, managing director at Major, Lindsey & Africa, told City AM there is often a difficulty in communication around salary for firms post-merger, especially when the UK and US counterparts operate on very different pay scales.

“The difficulty post-merger is the messaging around salary, particularly where the merger brings together two firms with very different salary scales. Bringing everyone immediately onto a US pay scale may require billable-hours expectations and charge-out rates to increase dramatically for one side of the merged firm, which is likely to be difficult to justify to either staff or clients,” Karnik said.

Karnik added, that for any law firm “facing the issue of two-tier salaries, they will likely have to be relatively open with associates about the business rationale behind them.”

“In such instances, over time we may see movement towards bringing all associates onto an equal salary scale, but I wonder whether it is more likely that we will see a third tier emerge, reflecting both the type and value of work associates are doing and whether they are meeting hours expectations comparable with those at a US firm,” she added.

“The key challenge will be maintaining those distinctions where associates feel they are doing broadly similar work, or working alongside each other on the same matters,” Karnik said.

Firms hike pay in the City

This year has already seen firms increase junior pay for their London offices, such as Quinn Emanuel, which in June increased salaries for its most junior lawyers by 5 per cent from £180,000 to £189,000 for the 2026 financial year, as its London office looked to align with pay increases at its US counterparts.

In July, Mischon de Reya also upped its salaries to £110,000 for its incoming cohort of junior lawyers.

articles.title: Tinkering Timms just wants to make it easier to claim benefits
articles.summary:
The Timms review does not recommend making any savings on welfare, instead it wants to develop a large and ineffective state machinery for doling out taxpayer money, says Emma Revell

Two welfare reviews in two weeks – Christmas has come early for wonks like me! The Timms review follows the Milburn review last week, which is an in-depth look  into Personal Independence Payments (PIP), the main disability payment for working age adults. 

It’s worth recapping where PIP fits into the benefits framework. There are three big categories of benefit for working age beneficiaries: unemployment, incapacity and disability. Unemployment and incapacity have been part of the benefits system for a long time, and depend usually on other income. 

Disability benefits are newer and were first introduced in the 1970s. PIP is the latest manifestation, and you can get between £30.30 and £194.60 per week. How much you get doesn’t depend on your income, rather it depends on whether you find it hard to do everyday tasks (such as preparing food) or to get around because of poor physical or mental health. 

The case load has risen dramatically compared to other benefits. In 1980/81, there were about 460,000 people receiving benefits for disability, compared to 1.2m on incapacity and 1.6m on unemployment benefits. In 2025/26, there were 7m people on disability benefits, with 3.2m working age adults on PIP (by contrast, there were 1.3m on unemployment benefits only and 3.7m on incapacity). As is widely reported, much of this rise has been people with mental health conditions. 

As a result, PIP costs are surging. In real terms (2026/27 prices) the cost of PIP is forecast to rise from £27.5bn in 2024/25 to £42.6bn in 2031/32. So, this is a big area of government spending that needs to be addressed. 

Enter Stephen Timms, whose report completely misses the moment. The whole report is about administrative tinkering to make it easier to claim PIP. 

Not that some change isn’t sensible. People with lifelong or degenerative conditions should be treated with greater dignity and it makes sense not to subject them to unnecessary ongoing reviews. Ensuring very disabled people have the support they need is also a sensible goal. 

But Timms makes no attempt to find savings and gives no acknowledgement of the rising caseload. There is a nod to ensuring PIP aligns with costs people face, but the report shies away from recommending that potential claimants will have to prove these costs. And there doesn’t appear to be an acknowledgement that people should receive less if they have no costs. The caseload could increase. The IFS have said that “evidence from past reforms tells us it would likely increase the number of claimants – and hence spending”.

The failure to engage seriously with eligibility criteria is a major flaw in the Timms report. It’s pretty clear that the current assessment is too open-ended, and that too many people with conditions that don’t have additional costs can still be awarded PIP. The Resolution Foundation has noted for example, that 1-in-6 working age claimants don’t have any additional costs for their disability. 

Now we have both Milburn and Timms reports, what should we expect? The main difference is that Milburn wants to completely remove PIP for under-25s, except in the case of severe disability. Any savings will then be redirected back into support. 

Last week I wrote about my  hope that the Milburn review’s tough love approach could help young people into work but I was worried that Labour will develop a large and ineffective state machinery that does little to improve the prospects for unemployed and inactive people. 

The Timms review simply increases my belief little will improve. Of course, both reports have been shaped by the politics of the Labour Party, who rebelled against even the most modest cuts proposed under Keir Starmer. In all likelihood, despite two reports launched with much fanfare, there will be no welfare savings under this government.

Daniel Herring is head of economic and fiscal policy at the Centre for Policy Studies

articles.title: Stockpiling? Prepping? Whatever you call it, don’t forget the luxuries
articles.summary:
What’s the hottest topic of conversation at work and among your friends? Is it Jensen Huang’s sex life? House prices? I’m willing to bet it’s stockpiling.

Call it prepping if you like, though I prefer to think of myself as a planner. ‘Prepper’ conjures up images of survivalists in woodland huts or eccentric billionaire compound-builders. Planning, on the other hand, is just sensible – and I’ve been doing it long before the government launched a campaign.

At every lunch and dinner I’ve been to in recent weeks, this topic has come up. Last week I was the guest speaker at a small dinner for banking and insurance execs. While there was plenty of discussion about regulation and the rise of AI, there was also time to admire the Amazon listing of a large solar-powered battery system – shown to me by a senior executive amid discussion of his water purification system.

Personally, I stocked up on ration packs, candles, torches, loo roll, batteries, gas stoves and first aid gear at the start of the year, all safely stashed away – hopefully never to be used.

Matches and a big torch are sensible precautions for a power cut but how bad would things have to be before I served my family a meal from the massive tub of freeze-dried food pouches? They have a shelf life of 25 years, by the way, and would be a last resort once the 48 tins of soup have run out.

Is prepping just a middle class sport?

Based on the conversations I’ve been having, I assumed that stockpiling had gone mainstream; that the government information campaign had worked. However, a new survey from YouGov shows that while 92 per cent of people have heard about the campaign, just 23 per cent have done anything about it.

The research found that the older you are, the more likely you have to taken action while just 14 per cent of 18-to-24-year-olds have prepped. I mean planned.

It turns out that preparing for a cyber-attack, pandemic or armed invasion is actually a minority sport and, among those that play, seemingly a competitive one. A feature in The Times this week looked at posh preppers with custom-made larders and tins of luxury food.

I suppose if we’re going to be forced into camping indoors and cooking via candlelight it couldn’t hurt to have a few jars of foie gras tucked away. Now we just have to consider the wine…

articles.title: Will Sadiq Khan run again?
articles.summary:
Sadiq Khan is keeping London guessing as to whether he will run for a fourth term as mayor. But this is not a parlour game that Khan can play forever, writes James Ford

If you are a lazy Hollywood director who wants to quickly convey that the focus of your movie has shifted to the UK’s capital city then there is really only one thing you can do. You play the Clash’s London Calling over a montage of red buses, black taxis and Big Ben. Job done. The Clash’s 1979 anthem is a leitmotif for London. There will have been little surprise, then, when London’s diminutive new Mayor picked “London Calling” as one of his six favourite songs when interviewed by the Rough Trade podcast back in 2016. 

However, I dare to suggest that were he to be asked to choose again today, Lord Khan might opt for a very different song by The Clash: 1982’s Should I Stay or Should I Go? That is certainly the question that is upper most in the Mayor’s mind currently. For some reason, Lord Khan has decided to keep London guessing about whether he will run for an unprecedented fourth term at City Hall. Indeed, he is threatening to leave London hanging until next May – only one year before the next set of City Hall elections – to make up his mind. 

A unique circumstance for London

It is not a position that the capital has been in before. We do not really do ‘term limits’ in the UK in the way that, say, a US President is constrained to eight years and no more. Technically a Mayor of London can go on and on and on until the electorate gets sick of them. Ken Livingstone was pretty clear about wanting to carry on being Mayor of London in 2008 and 2012 when he stood unsuccessfully against Boris Johnson. For his part, Boris was unambiguous in the other direction, ruling out seeking a third term early into his second term at City Hall. To drive the point home, in 2014 he announced he would be seeking a Westminster seat and a year later he became MP for Uxbridge, despite having a year left to run on his term of office. 

History, therefore, offers no lesson that ruling out another run makes any Mayor of London a lame duck. Johnson was still able to cut his proportion of council tax, introduce the ULEZ, and build more homes than either his predecessor or successor in his second term. Construction continued on the Elizabeth Line, the cycle hire scheme was expanded, and the rollout of the Boris Bus continued apace. Sadiq Khan probably wishes he could deliver so much in four years as a supposedly ‘lame duck’ Mayor.

Why is Khan procrastinating?

It is not clear what political objective is served by Sadiq’s continued procrastination. Other parties are not waiting for Sadiq to make his mind up before selecting their own would-be Mayors. Certainly, the London Labour Party does not benefit from the delay. If Sadiq makes his decision next May it could take until Labour Party Conference in September to run a ballot to select his replacement, which gives said candidate only eight months to introduce themselves to the London electorate (which is, of course, the largest group of voters in the UK to elect a single politician) and to wage an effective campaign. It is no surprise then that Len Duvall, Labour’s longest serving member of the London Assembly, recently stated Labour would “welcome a decision on [Khan’s] future sooner rather than later”.

I think that Khan has backed himself into a corner with this indecision. Deep down I suspect he knows what he wants to do. He has hinted at running again by recently declaring that being Mayor of London is the best job in politics. But, by dithering over an announcement he has created a Catch-22 situation for himself. If he announces he’s not standing it will look like he is worried about losing to James Cleverly and the Conservatives. But, if he is running yet again, it will now feel anticlimactic; as if Khan has just been seeking a little attention by teasing his exit. 

A third term?

I suspect Khan will run again, if only because it is hard to see what else he could do. He already has a peerage (the political equivalent of semi-retirement) but, one suspects, that serving in a mid-ranking Cabinet job would probably feel constrictive – perhaps even like a demotion – after he has been master of his own destiny in London for so long. Nor do I think he will have until May to tease London with this decision. Labour will demand an answer more quickly than that. Sadiq Khan is going to give us an encore, even if we don’t really want or need one. Should he stay? Probably not. Will he go? We aren’t that lucky. 

James Ford is a former adviser to Mayor of London Boris Johnson

articles.title: Top London investors call for stamp duty axe to stem FTSE exodus
articles.summary:
Top London investors have called on ministers to abolish stamp duty on shares and overhaul pension rules after catering giant Compass Group became the latest company to set out plans to swap its listing across the Atlantic this week.

Fund managers raised the alarm over the speed of exits from the London Stock Exchange after years of delistings and a dearth of IPOs.

UK-founded fintech Wise, Paddy Power-owner Flutter and equipment rental firm Ashtead are among those who have recently ditched primary listings in London in favour of New York. 

Georgina Hamilton, co-manager of the Polar Capital UK Value Opportunities Fund, urged ministers to abolish the stamp duty on shares and restrict ISA tax relief to require a minimum allocation to UK-listed equities, following the models of France and Italy.

She also encouraged the introduction of tax incentives to encourage UK pension funds to invest domestically, similar to that of Australia.

“The UK should rapidly move in line with other nations…protecting and growing the tax take,” she told City AM.

Ben Needham, a fund manager at Ninety One, said that scrapping stamp duty and reforming pension rules would improve sentiment towards the London Stock Exchange in the long run.

Their calls echo those of Andrea Rossi, boss of FTSE 100 investor M&G, who yesterday called on ministers to act against the wave of companies leaving the London Stock Exchange. Compass’s exit was a “warning about the health of the UK stock market”, he wrote in the Financial Times.

M&G, a shareholder in Compass, will vote against the move to swap its listing, Rossi said, adding that he did not believe switching value would deliver more value to investors.

Compass plots switch

The warnings come after catering giant Compass confirmed on Tuesday it is looking to switch its primary listing to New York in 2028, subject to shareholder approval.

Compass is the 17th largest firm on London’s blue-chip index, having a market value of roughly £43.6bn.

“It is a huge blow to UK capital markets, the UK government and those who benefit from government spending that another FTSE 100 company has been lost,” Hamilton said.

“This will reduce UK tax take and hamper the government’s ambition for growth. The stark reality is that Compass is not an isolated case and FTSE 100 boards across the country are actively considering this move,” she added.

Compass chairman Ian Meakins said the move reflects North America becoming a “powerful engine for growth for Compass” amounting for 75 per cent of its operating profit and holding over half of its 600,000 strong global workforce. 

Needham said Compass could address its valuation discount through share buybacks and claimed London’s slump in listings reflects the low point of a capital cycle, rather than a sign the market is losing its stance as an ideal place to list.

“Companies leaving the index is bad for the depth and health of the UK markets as a national asset class, but it doesn’t make UK equities a weaker proposition,” Needham said. “Our role, as investors in UK public markets, is to separate what is cheap because it has been tarnished by the ‘UK brush’ from what is cheap because it deserves to be.”

Is the grass greener?

Others in the City warned firms to be cautious over a move to New York, as they face losing the status and scale they hold in London.

“Unless you’re $10bn plus dollars in the US, you are a tiddler and you won’t get much attention,” said Patrick Sarch, head of UK public M&A at White & Case.

“Not much analyst following and you risk being badly understood, badly valued, not supported, not easily able to raise secondary.”

Of the 21 UK companies that have listed in the US since 2014, 13 have now delisted, three are trading above their IPO price, while the rest are on average trading down by 69 per cent, according to figures from the London Stock Exchange.

Needham also questioned the likelihood of what a switch to the US would achieve for Compass’s valuation, arguing it had already captured significant market share in the region while being listed in London and completed a vital equity raise in 2020.

“Put another way, how much extra free cash flow will ultimately come from a listing change?” he said.

articles.title: Natwest bets big on wealth as banks battle for Britain’s affluent
articles.summary:
Natwest has set out new ambitions plans for its wealth division. Samuel Norman takes a look at which banks are racing ahead in the battle for the mass affluent.

The turf war over Britain’s affluent savers has escalated after Natwest unveiled an aggressive blueprint for its private banking and wealth arm.

Top banks have raced to boost fee income in the face of falling interest rates that have tightened lending margins and turned attention to capital-light revenue streams.

Earlier this year, Natwest elbowed past its peers to snap up Evelyn Partners for £2.7bn – a deal hefty enough that the bank had to hit pause on further share buybacks. The bank has used the City wealth manager as a vehicle to expand its grip on the industry. 

The integration of Evelyn more than doubled its private bank’s assets under management and administration in the third quarter to £132.4bn, letting it rub shoulders with wealth management’s giants. 

On Wednesday, Natwest told investors it was now aiming to make its wealth arm the highest-returning unit across operations with 40 per cent return on tangible equity. It came alongside a goal to deliver assets under management of over £200bn by 2030. 

Natwest said the completion of Evelyn would open up its private bank Coutts to a broader range of financial tools, which it expects to bank an extra £50m in revenue from come 2030.

The group recorded a pre-tax profit of £2.2bn in the third quarter, broadly in line with consensus. But the bank faced pressure on net interest income, despite interest rates remaining higher than expected, which came under target.

Banks bring AI into the wealth space

Natwest’s fresh goals cast a long shadow over its peers with the likes of HSBC UK still angling to break into the £100bn assets club by 2030.

The bank, which has splashed out on a specialist wealth headquarters in London, has put a raft of roles on the chopping block with a push into artificial expansion. A current consultation is looking at halving the amount of management and specialist roles it has and cutting as much as 70 per cent of its financial advisers.

Natwest too promised to bear the axe on costs as part of its new strategy, with over £120m in savings, which mark around 10 per cent of its private bank’s cost base.

Around 50 per cent of this is from creating a “shared service model and processes” across the merged business. It will also push ahead with an AI financial planning assistant, set to be dubbed Eve, to slash the 7 to 14 hours advisers currently spend building a single client plan.

Barclays has also shifted focus to wealth expansion but has doubled down on organic growth, rather than through acquisitions after losing out on Evelyn Partners. The bank ended the third quarter with £56.5bn in assets under management, edging up from £52.9bn at the end of 2025.

It’s aiming for north of 25 per cent return on tangible equity in the unit, as a means to help the group-wide 12 per cent target. 

Meanwhile, Lloyds has faced hiccups in its wealth push with the departure of mass affluent chief Jo Harris within days of the launch of its new service. In October last year, the bank took control of the remaining stake in Schroders’ Personal Wealth, its partnership with the wealth manager. 

The wealth arena is set to mark another showdown for high street banks and their fintech rivals. Revolut bagged approval from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to broaden the scope of its wealth management operations in the UK earlier this year. 

The greenlight put it on the path to the launch of its private wealth services, which Bloomberg Intelligence forecast could generate £250m in annual revenue in the UK alone.

articles.title: Where did Anthropic go wrong in its first week of trading?
articles.summary:
Seven days ago, Anthropic’s co-founders rang the Nasdaq opening bell to mass euphoria.

Viewers of the most-anticipated listing of the year watched with awe as boss Dario Amodei’s gleaming smile stretched from ear to ear in New York’s Times Square.

The Claude maker sauntered onto Wall Street as the undisputed heavyweight of the AI boom, after retail investors jostled to secure shares in the lead up to its initial public offering. In the UK alone, investors snapped up $300m (£228m) worth of shares in what was a hugely oversubscribed offer.

The moment Wall Street opened, yet more investors rushed to get in on the action.h. After shares were priced at $83, way above the predicted $70 to $78 market range, they surged 34 per cent out of the gate to open at $111.50. 

This briefly crowned Anthropic with a market valuation of $2 trillion.

“Anthropic didn’t just beat expectations, it blew straight through them,” said Harley Salt, chief commercial officer at Thinkmarkets.

“It priced above the range, made the deal bigger, and still left $28 a share on the table on the opening trade. Investors who got an allocation at $83 had a very good day.”

But just one week later, sentiment had soured. By Tuesday’s close, the AI lab had plunged nearly 30 per cent from its peak to $81.9, taking it below IPO price for the first time. Things went from bad to worse by Wednesday’s open – the stock tumbled another nine per cent to $74, surrendering its trillion-dollar market cap status in the process.

This turned the company into a ‘broken IPO’ in just five trading sessions, five times faster than SpaceX suffered the same fate.

 The firm found itself caught in the crossfire of Nvidia’s leadership whiplash and weighed down by its own aggressive deal mechanics, detailing just how fragile investor appetite is.

The listing unravels

London-listed investment trusts who hold stakes in Anthropic also recorded losses, reversing their pre-IPO bounce.

Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, which has 9.3 per cent of funds invested in the firm, has fallen 6.4 per cent since last Thursday, while Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust has declined 4.8 per cent.

Analysts have pinned the slide on the handling of the share sale. By hiking the offer price and allowing it to open at $111.5, the underwriters running the listing burned through all pent-up investor demand on day one.

Banks also used their emergency reserve of extra shares to give the deal a boost, leaving nothing to prop up the stock once selling accelerated. 

“Anthropic’s underwriters cannot defend this level, after they exercised their full option to buy the stock on November 20th,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

“This stock will have a tough road ahead, after its bankers sold all stock last week, leaving it no ammunition to try and defend the IPO price. This is leaving the stock price in free fall.”

Wider problems

Meanwhile, the market was hit with a wave of unrestricted insider supply. Unlike SpaceX, more than half of Anthropic’s float went to existing venture backers, while employees were also cleared to sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings once trading began.

Regulatory filings also showed founders Dario and Daniela Amodei sold shares at the $83 price, triggering an evaporation of investor sentiment. Fellow co-founder Jack Clark, the former British tech journalist, also sold a small portion of their own shares.

“An IPO is often the culmination of months of hype, speculation and pent-up investor demand,” said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG.

“Once a company goes public, the excitement increasingly gives way to scrutiny of its financial performance, growth prospects and ability to justify its valuation… Anthropic will be no exception.”

The Claude maker’s missteps also collided with swelling scrutiny over its future profit. Nine-month revenue surged to $33.2bn in its latest financial results, but net losses widened to $104bn.

Investors quickly questioned future competitiveness – and baulked at the nearly $900bn in capital committed to computing power through to 2045.

The power of Jesen Huang

Anthropic debuted on a backdrop of volatility, led by Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, as the chipmaker ultimately cast a shadow over the AI lab’s first week on the public market.

Prior to its debut, eyes turned to Nvidia’s first earnings update since Huang’s resignation after reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Analysts argued investor’s response to earnings would paint a picture of appetite for wider AI and tech stocks.

But it was Huang’s shock return on Monday that threw Anthropic into wider market turmoil. Nvidia rocketed 31.4 per cent, while other firms including Intel, Micron and Broadcom, also swung back to gains as investors raced back to tech.

Anthropic failed to participate, which Brooks said reflects its area of the AI trade, as investors lack enthusiasm for labs which have “no track record of generating profits” unlike hyperscalers and chipmakers.

Where does this leave Anthropic?

Some analysts remain optimistic, with Oppenheimer, Canaccord Genuity and Wedbush maintaining a buy rating and price targets between $120 and $150.

But others do not share this sentiment, including those with holdings in firms including Alphabet and Amazon, among Anthropic’s largest backers. A further fall could lead to greater damage to their bottom lines.

Their top lines remain largely protected for now by multi-year contracts unless a broader AI slowdown eventually slows future demand for computing power.

David Morrison, senior market analyst noted that being the only frontier lab on the market, despite uncertainty over profits, grants it a market proposition.

 The current market environment looks unsettled, and their leading US rival, OpenAI, may be concerned that they have delayed their own IPO until next year,” he said.

“Things may have improved, but what if they get worse?”

Beauchamp added that some firms who suffer an “early setback” rebound to deliver “exceptional returns”.

“While there is no guarantee that Anthropic will follow the same pattern…  investors should not feel pressured into buying shares simply because they missed out on the initial listing,” he said.

“The opportunity to invest in a promising business rarely begins and ends on IPO day.”

articles.title: Thanksgiving on Ozempic: Clever tricks to survive the feast without offending the host
articles.summary:
With roughly 15% of Americans now reporting they have used a GLP-1 medication for weight loss, many Thanksgiving dinner plates may be a little less crowded this year.

Less "food noise" and a smaller appetite can make it tricky for people taking Ozempic, Wegovy or other glucagon-like peptide-1 drugs to navigate the etiquette of a traditionally large feast.

Patricia Araujo, a registered dietitian at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, shared her practical tips for enjoying the holiday meal — without overdoing it or making your host feel slighted.

HOW SKIPPING BREAKFAST TO SAVE ROOM FOR DINNER SHOCKS YOUR BLOOD SUGAR AND METABOLISM

Handling topics around food and diet can be challenging for patients on a GLP-1, according to Araujo.

While people shouldn’t feel pressured to disclose anything about their personal or medical history, it can be helpful to think ahead of time about how much they want to share, she advised.

If guests question why you aren't eating a certain dish or urge you to take seconds, Araujo recommends having a polite response ready, such as, "That looks delicious. Thank you for offering. I've had enough," or simply, "I'm comfortably full right now."

THE 8 HEALTHIEST BEANS YOU SHOULD BE EATING MORE OFTEN, ACCORDING TO NUTRITION EXPERT

People don’t necessarily have to tell others that they’re taking medication, she noted.

"Sometimes just sharing that they're working on eating smaller portions, or they're making some dietary changes, but still acknowledging that the food is great and that they are happy to be able to share that meal together can be enough," Araujo said.

The dietitian recommends that people on a GLP-1 should get plenty of nutrient-dense foods, with an emphasis on protein, fiber, vitamins and minerals.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Protein is important because it helps us maintain muscle mass when we're taking a GLP-1 and losing weight," she told Fox News Digital.

At a Thanksgiving table, good sources of protein include roasted turkey without the skin, beans, chickpeas, lentils and tofu, Araujo said.

"Fiber is really important for digestive health and to keep things moving," she said. "Good sources of fiber are fruits, vegetables and whole grains. At Thanksgiving, that can be roasted vegetables, a leafy salad, maybe a baked sweet potato."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Because GLP-1 medications suppress appetite and can trigger side effects like nausea or constipation, rich, high-fat dishes are much harder on the stomach.

Araujo advises being cautious with fried foods, heavy casseroles and sugary desserts — anything loaded with butter, oils or heavy creams — and sticking to "smaller quantities or smaller portion sizes" if you do indulge.

People taking Ozempic or similar medications who have a decreased appetite shouldn’t feel obligated to load up their plates or eat to the point of discomfort, the dietitian said.

"Giving ourselves permission to eat smaller portions, not feeling pressured to have to finish everything on our plate, will be helpful during Thanksgiving," she told Fox News Digital.

To help manage portion sizes, Araujo recommends taking a look at what's available before putting food on the plate.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Another tip is to use a smaller plate, like a salad plate, if that's available," she suggested, noting that it’s best to eat slowly, take small bites and listen to "satiety cues."

"If you still have food left on the plate, I think asking for a to-go dish is always a good idea," Araujo added.

For those who are concerned that healthy foods might not be available on Thanksgiving, it’s wise to contact the host ahead of time.

"You can ask about food choices, or even offer to bring your own dish," Araujo said. "Use that as an opportunity to bring something that's nutrient-dense that you know you can eat and tolerate and still enjoy the gathering, but feel well."

When possible, she recommends putting a healthy spin on traditional Thanksgiving dishes. "For example, we can make stuffing healthier by swapping the white bread for a whole-grain, high-fiber bread and adding in some vegetables."

articles.title: Norse Atlantic airline suspends all flights, on brink of bankruptcy amid rising fuel costs
articles.summary:
Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic suspended all flights Thursday as its board warned the company may imminently file for bankruptcy if it can't secure short-term financing.

"If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy," the company said in a statement.

The airline, which provides long-haul flights between the U.S. and Europe, said it had been discussing with investors a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution."

SHIPPING GIANT WARNS STRAIT OF HORMUZ CHAOS IS 'NEW NORMAL' AS TEHRAN SHIFTS 4M BARRELS

But, the company added, "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), which contracts jets from Norse through a wet-lease program, shifted all United Kingdom flights to its own Boeing 777 planes, claiming Norse announced the suspension with no notice as PIA passengers were preparing to board.

Norse, amid rising fuel costs from the Iran war, began leasing out its Boeing 787 fleet to other airlines as it struggled to make a profit on trans-Atlantic flights. In July, IndiGo, India's largest carrier, announced it would conclude its own wet-lease program with Norse by the end of October.

Norse's stock price plummeted and closed down 85%. Most of its value has been wiped out since the start of the year and the stock is now trading at $0.010.

Jet fuel prices in Europe have more than doubled since March amid fallout from the Iran war and the restrictions on oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz, where up to 20% of the world's petroleum flowed before the onset of the war in February.

The price increases have forced other airlines, most notably budget carrier Spirit Airlines, to shut down as well.

DUFFY BLAMES BIDEN-BUTTIGIEG TEAM FOR SPIRIT AIRLINES COLLAPSE AFTER BLOCKED MERGER

"Long-haul, low-cost is most exposed to high fuel costs as demand is subject to a high level of price elasticity. So maybe not a surprise," aviation analyst James Halstead told Reuters.

Norse Atlantic did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Your holiday shopping data needs a cleanup before Black Friday
articles.summary:
Your phone buzzes: "USPS: Your package could not be delivered due to an incomplete address. Update your details within 12 hours." You did order something last week. Probably several things. So your thumb hovers over the link. That's the whole trick.

Black Friday lands on Nov. 27 this year, and the holiday delivery rush is already underway. That gives scammers plenty of opportunities to send fake delivery alerts that arrive when you're expecting a package.

Meanwhile, your shopping habits and personal details may be circulating through data brokers. Here's how that information can make scams more convincing and what you can do to clean it up before the holiday shopping rush gets even busier.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?

Every time you shop online, sign up for a discount or share your contact information, you may add to a growing collection of personal data. Some businesses use that information for their own marketing, while others share certain details with advertising partners or data brokers.

Here's where some of that information comes from:

As I've covered before, loyalty programs and store memberships can contribute to the information companies collect about you. Add the personal details available through people-search sites, and someone looking to target you may find more information than you'd expect. The FTC explains that people-search companies collect information from multiple sources and sell reports containing personal details, sometimes including relatives' names and addresses.

You can use the free exposure scanner we recommend at CyberGuy.com to check whether your personal information appears on publicly searchable websites. Keep in mind that a free scan cannot uncover every private data broker database. The results might surprise you.

WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES

A fake delivery text doesn't need to know exactly what you ordered. During the holidays, plenty of people are expecting packages, so a message about a delivery problem can seem believable. Scammers often send these messages to large numbers of phone numbers without knowing anything about the recipients. However, personal information obtained from public sources or data brokers can help make some scams more convincing.

Here's how that information could be misused:

The FTC reported that fake package delivery problems, often involving messages impersonating USPS, were the most commonly reported type of text scam in 2024. The problem extends beyond package deliveries. According to FTC testimony released in March 2026, Americans reported $15.9 billion in fraud losses during 2025 across all scam categories. A typical fake delivery message directs you to a convincing website and asks you to pay a small redelivery fee. That payment request is the trap. The scammer wants your credit card details and may also try to collect other sensitive information. Here's something important to remember: USPS does not charge a fee for redelivery. Its legitimate text tracking service also requires you to request tracking information first, and those tracking messages do not contain links.

Data removal takes time. Brokers process opt-out requests on different schedules, and personal information can reappear even after it has been removed. Starting now gives you a chance to identify exposed information and begin requesting removals before the busiest shopping days arrive.

There is one important distinction. Removing your information from data brokers can reduce your exposure over time, but it cannot guarantee that scam texts will stop or prevent scammers from contacting you this holiday season. That's why data cleanup should go hand in hand with safer shopping and delivery habits.

You can get started in about 15 minutes, although completing data removal requests and having companies process them can take much longer.

Look up your name on people-search websites such as Spokeo, Whitepages or BeenVerified. Check whether your home address, phone number or relatives' information appears. If you find information you want removed, look for the site's opt-out instructions.

Check the privacy settings on the websites and apps you use most frequently. Look for options to limit promotional emails, personalized advertising and sharing with marketing partners. You can also review saved shipping addresses and remove outdated entries you no longer need. Keep in mind that deleting a saved address may not erase information retained in previous order records.

If a message claims there's a delivery problem, open the retailer's or shipping company's official app or website yourself. Check the tracking number and delivery status there. Do not enter payment details through a link in an unsolicited message, even if it includes your name or address.

Instead of spending hours submitting individual opt-out forms, an automated data removal service can send removal requests to hundreds of data brokers, depending on the provider and plan you choose. Some services also submit recurring removal requests to help address information that reappears. While no service can erase every piece of information about you online, it can help reduce your exposure. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Talk with your parents and other relatives about fake delivery messages. Make sure everyone knows to verify unexpected payment requests through the carrier's official website or app. For USPS specifically, explain that it does not charge redelivery fees. A message demanding immediate payment to release a package should raise suspicion.

If you receive a suspicious delivery message, don't respond or click the link. You can forward scam texts to 7726 (SPAM) and use your phone's reporting feature. For messages impersonating USPS, you can also report them to spam@uspis.gov. If you already entered your credit card information on a suspicious website, contact your card issuer immediately. Ask about blocking the card, disputing fraudulent charges and monitoring your account for unauthorized activity. You can also report the incident at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

What concerns me most about these fake delivery texts is how easily they blend into our holiday routines. When you're ordering gifts and waiting for packages, a message about a delivery problem can catch you at exactly the wrong moment. I also think we need to pay more attention to how much personal information is floating around online. Taking a few minutes to search your name, review your shopping accounts and start removing exposed information is worthwhile. But remember, even if you clean up your data, scammers can still reach you. My advice is simple: Never let an unexpected text dictate how you check on a package. Open the official app or website yourself and verify what's actually happening before you share a single detail.

Have you received a fake package delivery text that looked convincing, and how did you figure out it was a scam? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
