articles.title: Netanyahu declares corruption trial has 'fallen apart' after judges question key charges
articles.summary:
The decade-long legal battle against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suffered a major blow Wednesday after judges cast doubt on key corruption charges, prompting the Israeli leader to declare that his trial had "fallen apart" and demand an immediate end to the proceedings.

A three-judge panel at the Jerusalem District Court suggested that Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara consider dropping the most serious case against Netanyahu, questioned whether a criminal offense occurred in a second case and recommended resolving a third through a plea deal.

"Today, the trial fell apart," Netanyahu said in an evening address following the proceedings, according to The Times of Israel.

FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY

"Ten years ago, I said, ‘There will be nothing because there was nothing.’ But it took 10 years for this truth to be revealed to everyone," he said.

"Citizens of Israel, this trial must end immediately. And what also needs to end immediately is what came out of it — the hatred, the incitement, the division."

The court's intervention dealt a major setback to prosecutors more than six years after Netanyahu's trial began and roughly a decade after authorities launched the initial probe into him.

Judges had summoned Baharav-Miara to court Wednesday amid concerns over the strength of the prosecution's evidence and whether continuing the cases served the public interest.

"We’re now at a crossroad and need to rechart a new path," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told the attorney general, according to The New York Sun.

"Public interest dictates a need to rethink."

NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'

She and her colleagues, Judges Moshe Bar-Am and Oded Shaham, stressed that their comments were preliminary, did not constitute a verdict and applied only to Netanyahu because they still had to hear the other defendants’ testimony, The Jerusalem Post reported.

Baharav-Miara signaled that prosecutors would review the judges' recommendations and weigh their options.

Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust stemming from three corruption investigations.

Prosecutors announced the charges in November 2019 and formally filed the indictment in January 2020, and Netanyahu consistently denied wrongdoing.

The most serious charge, Case 4000, centers on allegations that Netanyahu granted regulatory favors to Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq in exchange for favorable coverage on the Walla news website, which was then controlled by businessman Shaul Elovitch.

Judges questioned whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence to secure a conviction. In Case 2000, prosecutors also allege Netanyahu negotiated for favorable coverage from Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper publisher Arnon Mozes in exchange for legislation to weaken rival newspaper Israel Hayom.

TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT

The proposed deal never materialized, and judges questioned whether a criminal offense had happened.

Case 1000 centers on allegations that Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, received almost $300,000 in gifts from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer.

Judges suggested resolving that case through an agreement. Zion Amir, an attorney who previously represented Netanyahu in the proceedings, rejected the prospect of a settlement.

In his address Wednesday, Netanyahu also accused investigators of pressuring his political associates to testify against him and described the toll the investigations had taken on his family. 

"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my wife and my sons," he said.

"Of delusional interrogations. Of character assassination. Of grave incitement that wounds the soul. Who will give us back those 10 years?"

Netanyahu, who requested a presidential pardon in November 2025 without admitting guilt, also called on his political opponents to set aside their differences and form a unity government.

"The boycotts must end, and now," Netanyahu said.

"I know what enormous and immediate dangers the State of Israel faces. There is only one way to deal with them. To unite in order to deal with them. We must unite to secure the future of Israel — no less than that, and immediately."

articles.title: Taking Ozempic or Wegovy could lead to extra cancer screenings, new study suggests
articles.summary:
Women taking popular weight loss medications may have higher breast density on mammograms and require more follow-up imaging, even when none of those abnormalities turn out to be cancer.

That's according to a new study scheduled for presentation at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, Nov. 29-Dec. 3, 2026, in Chicago.

The study examined 107 women, ages 34 to 79, who took GLP-1 receptor agonists, a class of drugs that includes Ozempic and Wegovy, for weight loss for at least one year.

POPULAR WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES

Participants lost between six and 107 pounds, with an average loss of 40 pounds. Researchers reviewed 214 screening mammograms taken before and after at least a year of treatment, according to the study.

Specialized software showed that breast density rose by at least one category in 62.5% of participants who took GLP-1s. Eight women moved up two density categories.

Radiologists also saw smaller breasts in roughly 58% to 79% of patients, depending on the reviewer, and increased skin thickening in about 9% to 18%.

Higher breast density is generally tied to a greater risk of breast cancer and can make tumors harder to spot on X-rays.

However, the pattern seen after weight loss likely reflects a shift in proportions rather than more dense tissue growing, according to lead author Dr. Eva C. Gombos, a diagnostic radiologist at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston.

POPULAR WEIGHT LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS

"It was surprising that 62.5% of women had increased BI-RADS breast density despite substantial weight loss, with no decreases observed," Gombos said in a release.

"This may reflect disproportionate loss of breast fat, causing a relative increase in mammographic density even as absolute fibroglandular volume decreases."

When a person loses significant fat from the breast, the remaining milk ducts and supportive tissue — known as fibroglandular tissue — can make up a larger share of what shows up on the image, even if the total amount of that tissue did not grow.

Gombos also noted that losing breast fat and volume can leave extra skin or skin folds, which may help explain why skin and connective tissue strands looked more prominent on some scans.

Nearly 22.4% of the women were called back for additional imaging after screening, compared with an average U.S. recall rate of about 10%.

Two women had technical recalls to repeat scans due to positioning or imaging issues. Four women were referred for biopsies, and all four came back benign. All other callbacks also turned out to be benign or negative, including three simple cysts.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Gombos emphasized that the findings should not pose a concern for women taking GLP-1 drugs or cause them to skip routine screenings.

Whether these density shifts carry any long-term change in breast cancer risk remains unclear and needs more research.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The study was retrospective and looked back at medical records rather than following patients forward in a controlled trial, the researchers noted.

It did not establish whether the imaging changes affect long-term breast cancer risk.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Gombos recommends that women tell their breast imaging team if they use GLP-1 medications or have recently lost a significant amount of weight because it helps technologists and radiologists more accurately compare new scans to older ones.

Novo Nordisk, maker of Ozempic and Wegovy, emphasized that it continuously monitors the safety profile of its medicines, reviewing emerging data as it becomes available.

"Individuals respond to treatment uniquely based on multiple biological and lifestyle factors, which means outcomes can vary from person to person," a spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

"We recommend that all patients maintain close contact with their healthcare professional to discuss any questions or concerns about their treatment, and for ongoing guidance and careful monitoring."

articles.title: Doctors warn of lead exposure health risks after controversial Army detonation in Iowa
articles.summary:
The U.S. Army blew up about five tons of lead azide, a toxic bomb-making chemical, in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, raising concerns over airborne heavy-metal exposure.

The mission was reportedly necessary because the substances were "unstable" and liable to explode if tampered with.

While a Trump administration official reported that the detonation exceeded expectations by achieving maximum mitigation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) warned that residents within 20 miles should continue to shelter in place to avoid inhaling lead dust, and should follow EPA safety guidance "until given the all clear by officials."

IOWA RESIDENTS NEAR AMMUNITION PLANT TOLD TO VACATE BEFORE ARMY DETONATES 5 TONS OF BOMB-MAKING CHEMICALS

"[The] EPA has been on the ground in Iowa BEFORE the controlled detonation, we will be here DURING the detonation, and we will be here for as long as necessary AFTER detonation to ensure communities are safe," the Environmental Protection Agency said prior to the blast.

The agency predicted a brief increase in lead in the air above Middletown, as officials in Iowa and Missouri warned of potential exposure to toxic lead dust.

According to Mayo Clinic, even small amounts of lead can cause serious health problems. Long-term buildup of lead in the body can get stored and slowly re-enter the bloodstream over time.

AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY

At very high levels, lead can damage the kidneys and nervous system in both children and adults, leading to complications in the brain, seizures, neuropsychiatric symptoms and unconsciousness.

Children under 6 years old are the most susceptible, as lead poisoning can severely impact development of their bodies and brains.

According to the Iowa Farm Bureau, Iowa leads the nation in producing corn, pigs, eggs, ethanol and biodiesel — commodities that end up in everyday household products." The state also ranks No. 2 in soybean production and cover crops.

One Iowa farmer, Doug Seyb, spoke with PBS about his concern that the detonation could impact his nearby farm, including his cows out at pasture and local ponds that fill the farm's water tank.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The public fears that lead could eventually enter the food supply through crops grown in contaminated soil and livestock raised on contaminated water.

Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician, medical toxicologist and Fox News medical contributor, confirmed that lead being dispersed into the air is "not a small deal."

"Lead has no beneficial role in human physiology," she said. "In fact, lead in the human body can really mess with biology."

People who eat fresh produce already take in trace amounts of heavy metals like lead, which is widespread in soil — but detonating a "tremendous amount" of the toxic metal raises the risk of dangerous exposure, Widmer warned.

AGGRESSIVE CANCER TYPE LINKED TO COMMON CHEMICAL EXPOSURE IN NEW STUDY

"If there is an enormous amount that is going to be contaminating the food supply, the water, the air that people are breathing in, this is very concerning," she said.

Widmer suggested that Americans near the detonation site should continue to listen to guidance to shelter in place, keep windows closed, and turn on ventilation or air purifying systems.

"We know that lead is dangerous for humans, but we don't know how much, or if any, lead they're being exposed to," she said. "It could be none. It could a ton."

The EPA reported no levels of lead in the air 30 minutes after the detonation, but Widmer noted that just because the blow is over doesn't mean there is no lingering impact.

"Lead inhalation is one of the most efficient ways that lead can be dispersed into the human body," she said, adding that even if it's not inhaled, it can be dispersed into the soil. "It can stay in soil, it could stay in water," the doctor said.

"The very concerning thing is that lead can have negative effects on the human body without even showing any symptoms," she said. "There's still going to have to be testing. Follow-up is really key here."

Symptoms in adults can include the following, according to Cleveland Clinic.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Among children, lead exposure can cause the following effects.

Besides breathing in the toxic lead dust dispersed through the air, fallen particles contaminating water and soil can also pose a health risk, experts say.

Those who believe they have been exposed to lead, even without showing symptoms, should visit a healthcare provider for a blood test to check for exposure and lead levels, Widmer advised.

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

articles.title: Putin's war death toll reportedly tops 700,000 as Russia scrambles for recruits
articles.summary:
The Kremlin on Wednesday dismissed a new investigation estimating that at least 700,000 Russian troops have died in President Vladimir Putin's war against Ukraine, as experts warn that mounting military losses are undermining Moscow's ability to sustain its offensive.

The findings, published Monday by independent Russian news outlets Meduza and Mediazona, are based on leaked Russian government records and statistical analysis.

"The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the Russian Defense Ministry," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Wednesday, according to The Moscow Times.

PUTIN'S WAR MACHINE TIED TO TROUBLING RECRUITMENT OF YOUNG WOMEN AS NEW DEALS EMERGE

Peskov urged reporters to disregard other figures but offered no updated official death toll.

The investigation draws on records obtained by the hacking groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow after they breached Russia's federal statistics agency, Rosstat.

Researchers identified at least 490,000 registered military deaths by late September 2026. However, delays in registering fatalities and soldiers who remain officially listed as missing but are believed to be dead led researchers to estimate that the actual toll had likely reached 700,000 or more by that time.

Keti Korkiya, a research analyst at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital that she considered the estimate of more than 700,000 Russian military deaths plausible, noting that Britain's defense chief had already put the death toll above half a million in September. "The biggest uncertainty is how many of the soldiers still listed as missing have died," Korkiya said.

"Russia can keep fighting despite these losses," she added. "It still recruits tens of thousands of men a month, and this week the Duma approved a budget that devotes 35% of next year’s federal spending to defense. The war is straining Russia’s economy, but that pressure is unlikely to force Putin to stop fighting anytime soon."

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

The findings also raise questions about Russia's ability to replenish its forces nearly five years into the war.

A European intelligence source who spoke to Fox News Digital last week described Russia's efforts to replenish its forces as a form of "hidden mobilization," with recruiters approaching people on the streets, including homeless individuals, and offering them military contracts.

The source said Russia continues to recruit prisoners and target people struggling with financial difficulties, including those with outstanding debts or unpaid child support, effectively offering military service as "a kind of a social deal."

The recruitment strategy, the source said, is increasingly geared toward "more quantity, less quality."

The mounting losses have yielded limited territorial gains for Moscow, according to a separate July 1 report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

The report, authored by Seth G. Jones and Riley McCabe, estimated that Russia had suffered approximately 1.4 million battlefield casualties, including as many as 450,000 deaths, by mid-2026.

Ukraine has also suffered significant military losses. The same CSIS report estimated that between 125,000 and 150,000 Ukrainian troops had been killed between February 2022 and June 2026, with total military casualties reaching between 525,000 and 625,000.

Despite mounting military and economic pressures, the researchers warned that Putin was unlikely to abandon his ambitions in Ukraine without facing additional costs.

"Without greater costs in blood and treasure, Putin is likely to keep fighting," Jones and McCabe wrote.

Korkiya said Putin's decision to continue fighting reflects his belief that Moscow can outlast both Kyiv and its Western allies. "Putin has had opportunities to stop the fighting. When Ukraine agreed to a U.S. proposal for a 30-day ceasefire, he chose to keep fighting," she said.

"He still believes Russia can bear these losses longer than Ukraine and its allies can hold out. So far, even the deaths of hundreds of thousands of his own soldiers haven’t changed that calculation."

Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs echoed that assessment in an interview with Fox News Digital on Monday, arguing that Western leaders risk underestimating the ideological and religious beliefs driving Russia's war.

"We are too pragmatic and rational in the West," Rinkēvičs said.

RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH NUCLEAR-CAPABLE SATELLITE WITHIN WEEKS, WESTERN INTELLIGENCE WARNS: REPORT

He pointed to the concept of Russia as the "Third Rome" and the belief in its historical mission to serve as the protector of Christianity, arguing that such ideological convictions also drive Moscow's foreign policy and its war against Ukraine.

"Russia is using all the diplomatic kind of decoys simply to prolong the war," Rinkēvičs said.

The Latvian president suggested that a potential diplomatic opening could emerge in the spring or summer of 2027, provided Ukraine withstands Russia's winter campaign.

"Currently, Russia explores diplomatic efforts in order to prolong the war, not to end," he said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to target Russian military assets deep inside the country.

Ukraine's General Staff said Wednesday that its forces had damaged five Russian military aircraft at the Savasleyka airbase in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, including three MiG-31 fighters and two Su-34 fighter-bombers, according to an official Ukrainian military statement.

Russia did not immediately comment on the Ukrainian claims, Reuters reported Wednesday.

The ongoing fighting has also heightened concerns about the war spilling into NATO territory.

Poland's military reported Tuesday that a Russian drone had briefly entered Polish airspace during an overnight attack on western Ukraine. The incident came four days after three Russian cruise missiles landed in Poland.

Reuters contributed to this story.

articles.title: Can hackers still read Gmail after a password change?
articles.summary:
You change your Gmail password after noticing something suspicious. You sign out of unfamiliar devices and figure your account should be safe again. But what if someone could still read your Gmail after a password change? That's the unsettling claim behind Remus Stealer, a malware service being marketed to cybercriminals. Its developers claim they can keep accessing Gmail messages even after someone resets their password and revokes existing sessions.

However, security researchers have not independently verified those claims, and Google disputes the suggestion that the malware exploits a Gmail security flaw. The company says this type of attack targets infected devices rather than Gmail itself. Google also warns that changing your password may not solve the problem if malware remains active on your computer. Here's what the investigation uncovered and how to protect your inbox.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED

Security researchers at Hudson Rock examined promotional materials for Remus Stealer, a type of malware designed to collect sensitive information from infected computers. In a November 9 report, the company described a new feature advertised in version 1.3.9 of the malware. The developers claim it allows criminals to open a compromised Gmail inbox directly from their control dashboard. The promotional screenshots show lists of emails and individual messages. There's also a "Mail" option connected to records of infected devices. According to the developers, criminals can retrieve email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files.

The developers make an even more concerning claim. They say changing a Google password or revoking existing sessions won't necessarily stop someone from accessing the mailbox. They also advertise a way to share mailbox access with other criminals through links. Think about what that could mean if the claims prove true. Someone with access to your Gmail could potentially read private conversations or collect password reset messages for other accounts. However, these claims come from the people selling the malware. Independent researchers have yet to demonstrate that the feature works as advertised.

Hudson Rock contacted the malware developer and spoke with someone who claimed to have used the Gmail feature. That person said they could still access an inbox after closing the browser, resetting a session and changing the Google account password. The developer also described a technique involving browser memory but didn't provide enough technical information to verify it. There are important limits to the investigation.

Hudson Rock did not reverse engineer the feature or conduct controlled testing after a complete account recovery. Researchers also couldn't independently verify the customer's claims. Most importantly, the investigation never established that criminals could retrieve newly arriving emails after someone had properly secured their Google account. The screenshots demonstrate that the service advertises a Gmail-reading interface. They don't prove that Remus can defeat Google's protections after a full recovery. There's also no evidence in the report of a previously unknown Gmail security vulnerability.

Researchers also could not rule out other explanations, including incomplete session revocation, previously collected messages or unauthorized access that remained active through another route. Without controlled testing, there's no way to confirm exactly how the advertised feature operates.

NEW AI MALWARE RANKS VICTIMS BY HOW MUCH THEY'RE WORTH

We reached out to Google about the research, and the company rejected the suggestion that the reported activity involved a vulnerability in Gmail. A Google spokesperson said: "Attacks involving infostealer malware that target session tokens on personal devices are not new, and there is no Gmail or Google vulnerability at play here. We routinely upgrade our built-in defenses to protect users against session theft and automatically secure accounts when we detect suspicious activity. Users can invalidate stolen sessions by removing malware from the affected device and revoking active sessions via g.co/mydevices."

Google explained that this kind of attack targets infected personal devices rather than exploiting Gmail itself. The company also highlighted something especially important for anyone recovering from malware. If the infection remains on a computer when someone resets their password, the malware could capture the new login session. That means a fresh password alone may not solve the problem. Google recommends removing the malware before signing back in on the affected device. From a separate, trusted device, you should also change your password, revoke suspicious sessions through Google's device activity page at myaccount.google.com/device-activity and review your account using Security Checkup at myaccount.google.com/security-checkup. The infected computer should remain disconnected until the threat has been removed.

The company says it regularly strengthens its defenses against stolen sessions. Those protections include frequent cookie rotation and additional authentication checks when someone attempts sensitive account changes. Google also highlighted Device Bound Session Credentials, a Chrome security technology designed to make stolen session cookies harder to reuse on another device. This protection applies to supported Chrome sessions, with availability depending on the platform and service. These protections help reduce the risk of account theft, although they don't eliminate every possible malware attack.

You probably open Gmail every day without typing your password. That's because your browser remembers that you've already signed in. Behind the scenes, browsers and applications use session cookies or authentication tokens to maintain access to accounts. These digital credentials help keep you signed in without repeatedly entering your password. Unfortunately, criminals know how valuable that information can be. Infostealer malware can target stored authentication data on an infected computer. If an attacker obtains a valid session, they may be able to access an account without entering the password again. That can also undermine the protection you'd normally expect from two-step verification because the legitimate account holder has already completed the sign-in process.

However, a stolen session doesn't automatically give someone unlimited access. Google can invalidate sessions, and some sensitive actions require additional verification. Google's documentation explains that changing a password generally revokes OAuth access and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions, although certain exceptions apply. Google also notes that password changes sign people out of most devices, but some trusted devices and third-party connections may remain signed in. Those exceptions do not prove that Remus uses any of these methods. The concern with an infected computer is that malware may capture fresh authentication information when you sign in again. That's why securing the computer and reviewing account access are essential parts of recovery.

An unfamiliar Google security alert deserves attention, especially if you haven't signed in from a new device. You should also investigate password reset messages you never requested. These can indicate that someone is attempting to access another account connected to your email address, although an unexpected reset message alone doesn't prove an account has been compromised.

Other warning signs include missing messages or people telling you they received strange emails from your address. Check your Sent folder for messages you didn't write. You might also discover forwarding rules or account recovery settings you don't remember changing. If something looks suspicious, open your Google account directly rather than following a link in an unexpected message.

If you suspect that someone has accessed your Gmail, take action promptly. The goal is to secure your account while preventing malware from stealing fresh login information. Google emphasizes that removing the infection and revoking compromised sessions are both essential. You can begin securing your account from a trusted device while keeping the suspected infected computer offline.

If you believe your computer has been infected, disconnect it from the internet. Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing your important accounts.

Strong antivirus protection with real-time scanning can help prevent infostealers from gaining access in the first place. However, no antivirus program can guarantee that every threat will be detected. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

Use a trusted device to secure your Google account. If you suspect that malware stole your login information, change your password promptly and make sure the infected computer cannot capture another session. Do not sign back into Google on the suspected infected computer until you have removed the malware.

Google notes that several sessions can appear under the same device name. Review each one and sign out of any you cannot confidently identify. If you've already changed your password while malware was still running, make sure the infected device has been cleaned or remains offline, then change your password again from a trusted device and review active sessions once more.

A criminal who gains access to your Gmail may change settings so incoming messages get forwarded to another email address. That could allow someone to receive copies of new messages even after you change your password. Google requires verification when someone adds a new forwarding address, but you should still check for forwarding that may have been configured without your knowledge.

To check your Gmail settings on a computer:

Some third-party applications can access parts of your Google account after you grant permission. If an unfamiliar app has access to your Gmail, it deserves a closer look.

You can also read my CyberGuy guide on apps accessing your Google account for additional instructions.

Google recommends several protections that can make account takeovers harder.

Passkeys offer stronger sign-in security, but they cannot remove an existing infection or automatically prevent theft of an already authenticated session. Google's Advanced Protection Program adds stricter account safeguards, including tighter restrictions on third-party access.

Remember how many online services use your email address for account recovery. If criminals accessed your mailbox, they may have seen verification messages from other services. Review important accounts for unfamiliar activity. Pay particular attention to unexpected password changes or security alerts.

If you reused your Google password anywhere else, change those passwords too. Use unique credentials for every important account, and consider a password manager to keep track of them. For additional protection, my CyberGuy article on identity thieves who don't need your password explains other ways criminals try to get around traditional account security.

For years, changing your password has been one of the first things I've recommended when an online account gets compromised. I still believe that's essential. But this investigation highlights something many people overlook. If malware is running on your computer, it may be able to steal fresh login information after you've changed your password. What concerns me is how much of our digital lives depend on a single Gmail account. Think about the personal messages sitting in your inbox and the accounts that rely on your email for password recovery.

Someone who gains access could potentially create problems well beyond your inbox. Google's response makes an important distinction. This is a threat involving malware on infected devices, not a newly demonstrated vulnerability in Gmail. We should also remember that the most alarming claims about this malware have yet to be independently verified. There's a big difference between what criminals advertise and what security researchers can actually demonstrate.

My advice is to take account security seriously without panicking over an unproven claim. Keep strong antivirus protection running on your devices and pay attention to suspicious account activity. If you suspect an infection, make sure the malware has been removed before trusting a fresh login. Then change your password from a trusted device and revoke any suspicious sessions. Those extra steps can help prevent someone from regaining access to your account.

articles.title: Tech billionaire plans 1,000-year floating city at sea
articles.summary:
How frustrated would you have to be with government red tape to decide the ocean looks like a better place to build a factory? Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey has an answer. He wants to create a massive floating industrial city where American companies could operate beyond certain state and local restrictions.

The project is called SLAB, and Luckey says it would have a design life of 1,000 years. That's a pretty extraordinary promise for something sitting in the middle of the ocean. However, the reasoning behind the project may be even more surprising than the structure itself. We discussed Luckey's ambitious plans in detail on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast" at cyberguy.com/podcast. So, what exactly is he planning to build, and could moving American industry offshore really solve the problems he's trying to escape?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS

Palmer Luckey, the founder of Oculus and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has revealed plans for a floating industrial platform called SLAB. In a November 18 post on X, Luckey explained that he began developing the project after Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014. He used some of the money from that sale to pursue an idea that has fascinated technology entrepreneurs for years.

The concept is known as seasteading. It involves building permanent structures on the ocean where people can live or operate businesses outside some of the restrictions that apply on land. Luckey's version focuses heavily on American industry. He wants to create a place where companies could conduct activities that face significant regulatory hurdles on the mainland. The illustration accompanying his announcement shows an enormous platform rising above the ocean with buildings and industrial facilities on top.

AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY

Luckey believes government regulations have made it unnecessarily difficult for certain industries to operate in the United States. His proposed solution is to move some of those operations offshore. He specifically mentioned metal processing and oil refining. He also identified desalination and medical research as possible activities for SLAB. In his announcement, Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen American industry by creating a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations."

His argument is that companies could operate more efficiently if they avoided certain state and local restrictions. He also wants the offshore platform to be cheaper than building comparable facilities on land, although he has not publicly demonstrated that the economics would work. There is also a more controversial possibility. In a separate exchange on X, Luckey suggested that offshore facilities could provide access to medical treatments currently prohibited in the United States. That raises difficult questions about patient safety and whether those activities could legally take place offshore.

Luckey says he and several close friends funded SLAB at a $1 billion valuation back in 2017. However, that figure refers to the project's reported valuation at the time. It does not establish that $1 billion has been spent building it. He also says the project has made significant progress, although considerable work remains. So far, he has not publicly disclosed a confirmed construction schedule or a precise location for the proposed platform.

Interestingly, Luckey only decided to discuss SLAB publicly after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He pushed back on that description, saying the project was much older and considerably more ambitious. His comments suggest that data centers could be part of the broader concept, but SLAB was conceived for other industrial activities as well.

This is where Luckey's proposal runs into some complicated legal questions. According to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, most coastal states, including California, have jurisdiction over submerged lands extending approximately three nautical miles offshore. Beyond that boundary, federal authority becomes especially important. The United States has a territorial sea extending 12 nautical miles from its coastal baselines. It also maintains an exclusive economic zone extending up to 200 nautical miles offshore.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains that the federal government retains authority over certain offshore structures and activities within that zone. Consequently, moving a business beyond California's coastal boundary would not automatically eliminate federal oversight. Environmental requirements and maritime regulations could still apply. The legal picture would also depend on whether SLAB floats freely, anchors to the ocean floor or operates under a particular country's registration. Luckey has yet to explain exactly how the platform would navigate those requirements.

Building a permanent industrial community offshore presents extraordinary engineering challenges. Saltwater gradually corrodes exposed structures, and powerful storms can place enormous stress on offshore installations. Maintaining a facility for centuries would require substantial engineering and ongoing repairs. Then there is the expense of running an industrial operation at sea. Workers would need transportation to the platform, while supplies and equipment would have to travel across the water.

That makes Luckey's goal of operating more cheaply than comparable land-based facilities particularly ambitious. A 1,000-year design life is also a target rather than a demonstrated lifespan. Until Luckey releases detailed engineering evidence, there is no way to independently verify whether SLAB could meet that goal.

California has long been associated with technological innovation, yet it also has extensive environmental and land-use regulations. Some businesses argue that permitting requirements make industrial development more expensive and time-consuming. Luckey's proposal brings that debate into focus. Moving industrial activity offshore would be a drastic response to regulatory frustration. However, the idea also raises a question worth asking: Have some regulations become so burdensome that entrepreneurs would rather build at sea than navigate the approval process on land?

Of course, industries involving hazardous chemicals or experimental medical treatments require serious oversight. Those protections help prevent accidents and protect public health. At the same time, regulations can become unnecessarily complicated or outdated. Governments need to examine whether their approval processes encourage responsible innovation or create obstacles that serve little practical purpose. Luckey has not identified the specific California laws he hopes to avoid. For now, his project highlights a broader argument about how America regulates industrial development. Whether SLAB becomes a functioning offshore community remains to be seen.

I find the whole idea fascinating, but something about it also strikes me as completely absurd. Have we really reached a point where building a giant industrial platform in the ocean sounds more appealing than dealing with government regulations on land? California, in particular, should be paying attention. This is a state that helped create Silicon Valley, yet we're now talking about taking American industry offshore to escape regulatory headaches. I'm certainly not suggesting we eliminate important environmental or safety protections. But there's a point where excessive regulation can start working against the very innovation we should be encouraging. I'd much rather see American businesses building here, creating jobs and developing new technology without unnecessary roadblocks. Luckey still has a tremendous amount to prove before SLAB becomes reality. But the fact that he's seriously pursuing this idea should give policymakers something to think about. For more on this story and our discussion about the future of American innovation, listen to The CyberGuy Report Podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/.

Would you support American companies moving industrial operations offshore to avoid certain regulations, or should lawmakers focus on reforming those regulations here at home? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
