articles.title: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
articles.summary:
Chris McGrath/Getty

Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

Chris Bowen, the COP31 president of negotiations and Australia’s Minister for Climate Change, speaks to the media after the final session during the second overtime day of the climate talks.
Chris McGrath/Getty

No mention of the ‘F’ word

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”.

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

Activist Greta Thunberg attends a protest at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
Burak Kara/Getty

The “COP of action” fails to deliver

This year’s climate summit was billed as an “implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as “president of negotiations”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

What about money for adaptation?

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water”. He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”.

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Press and participants watch as a man dressed as a dinosaur performs as part of the Fossil Of The Day award at the COP31 UN climate summit.
Burak Kara/Getty Images

Defending the science

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

IPCC chair Jim Skea at the opening ceremony of COP31. Previously, he described the stymied outcome of the meeting in Ethiopia as frustrating and disappointing.
Chris McGrath/Getty Images

Australia on the global stage

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “nothing on the field” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.”

Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.”

Are COP summits still worthwhile?

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”.

Jacqueline Peel receives funding from the Australian Research Council. She is affiliated with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, serving as a coordinating lead author in Working Group III (mitigation) for the Seventh Assessment Report.

Kathryn Bowen receives funding from Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water, the World Health Organisation, Wellcome, the Global Fund, Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility, Asian Development Bank and World Bank. She is affiliated with the Port Philip EcoCentre and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change where she is a lead author for the Sixth and Seventh Assessment Reports (Working Group II - Impacts, Vulnerability and Adaptation).

articles.title: Andy Burnham’s Brussels deal throws up a paradox for both sides in the EU debate
articles.summary:
At a summit in Brussels this month, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham revealed breakthroughs in the UK-EU “reset” begun under his predecessor Keir Starmer.

The summit produced agreement on several important issues. New rules from March 2028 will remove the need for certification of animal and food products, UK and EU emissions trading systems (ETS) will be linked, and a youth experience scheme will enable up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds to work and study in the UK or EU.

And in the meantime, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to working towards a closer relationship.

Yet the announcement came in for criticism from the political right. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued that Burnham had “oversold” the deal when he presented it to parliament. She said the prime minister was trying to take Britain “back to 2015”.

Meanwhile, Reform UK’s leader Nigel Farage claimed the agreement amounted to a betrayal of Brexit.

A lightning rod for criticism

Notably, the reset appears to be garnering more intense criticism than it did under Starmer. One reason for this is that the stakes are now higher. Burnham has already sought to shift the dial on Europe and has openly flirted with the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU.

Both sides see the summit an opportunity to lay the groundwork for the bigger fight to come.

Criticism of the deal is already having a chilling effect. Burnham has been noticeably more coy in his language about rejoining the EU, insisting in his remarks to the House of Commons that he would seek to rejoin only if it was in the UK’s interests – and on the back of a new referendum.

But the criticism from the Conservatives and Reform of the reset announcement misses the point. What it actually does is highlight the limitations of being outside the EU.

Badenoch’s claim that Burnham oversold the deal partly reflects the numbers involved, which look small but are in fact significant. The promised 0.4% increase in GDP amounts to a significant economic boost at a time when UK growth has been sluggish. This is hardly trivial.

Meanwhile, the non-EU trade deals preferred by Reform and the Conservatives have resulted in a far smaller contributon to UK growth than Burnham’s reset deal. UK accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), for instance, is associated with an anticipated boost to GDP just one tenth the size of the current reset.

Badenoch responded to Burnham’s statement on the summit saying he was making Britain a ‘rule-taker’.

And yes, Badenoch may be right that the figure is not going to change the world. But this reflects the limitations imposed by Brexit more than anything else.

Back in 2016, the Leave campaign claimed that withdrawing from the EU would not disproportionately affect the trading relationship with the bloc. That turned out to be illusory, as the EU correctly surmised that affording the UK special treatment would undermine the value of membership and lead to the disintegration of the internal market.

Thus, the EU has opposed efforts by the UK to negotiate piecemeal integration into the single market – which it describes as “cherry picking”. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it has only been willing to negotiate on specific areas where it sees a discernible benefit for the bloc.

The real limitation of Burnham’s deal is not a lack of ambition, but the strictures imposed by Brexit. And getting that 0.4% figure up would mean being open to more radical forms of re-engagement – as Burnham is indeed doing. (Estimates of the economic benefits of rejoining the EU are between 4%-6% of GDP).

Badenoch also notes, correctly, that the deal requires the UK to align with EU rules. But again, this is a symptom of Brexit, which removed the UK from EU decision-making forums and from any say over these rules. Since Brexit, the UK has continued to mimic EU rules in many areas – including state aid – without having any influence over them.

Solving the UK’s rule-taker problem arguably points to the benefits of rejoining. This would return the UK’s place within the EU’s legislative process and solve the so-called “democratic deficit” afflicting third-party countries participating in the internal market.

The simultaneous conversations on the reset and rejoining the EU result in a paradox for both sides. For the right, criticising Burnham’s agreement offers a means of heading off further moves towards the EU. But it also highlights the very real limitations of what is possible outside that framework.

And for Burnham and Labour europhiles, the need to tout the agreement as a success misses a clear opportunity to highlight the limits of Brexit and the benefits of rejoining.

Both sides, in their own way, miss what the reset really makes clear. That is that the deal exposes the continued trade-offs of Brexit and the limits of what is possible outside the EU.

Hence the political right may inadvertently bolster the case for rejoining – while Labour proudly showcases what can be achieved from the outside.

Benjamin Martill is affiliated with Chatham House and the Independent Commission on UK-EU Relations and has previously received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme.

articles.title: Half a million books are going into UK prisons – but there are still barriers to reading that need to be tackled
articles.summary:
For people in prison, reading can build confidence, provide a sense of achievement, offer imaginative escape and help maintain connections with family, other prisoners and the wider world.

In November 2026, half a million books were distributed across UK prisons in an ambitious initiative led by The Reading Agency. The programme comes towards the end the National Year of Reading 2026, a campaign to encourage people across the UK to rediscover reading for pleasure and make it part of everyday life.

It is a remarkable investment in reading. But getting books into prisons is only part of the challenge. How do we ensure people have the confidence, opportunity and choice to read them?

Our research has found that how people see themselves as readers can shape their engagement with books. If reading for pleasure is to become a lasting part of prison life, we need to understand these barriers and offer different ways to overcome them.

In focus groups with people in prison, we encountered complicated relationships with reading. Some participants were interested in books but lacked confidence in their abilities. Others struggled to see themselves as readers at all. Reading aloud or discussing a text in front of others could feel exposing, particularly for those uncertain about their skills.

The prison environment presents further challenges. Restricted movement, institutional routines and limited access to libraries can leave people with little control over what, when and how they read. An interest in books does not always translate into an opportunity to engage with them.

Group discussions and author visits can be valuable, but not everyone feels comfortable participating nor has permission to attend. For some, the freedom to read privately, reflect without scrutiny and progress at their own pace may be just as important.

Bringing the book club into the cell

These findings informed the development of the University of Hull’s digital book club for readers and writers, launched earlier this year.

Delivered through in-cell technology that is available in more than 90 prisons across England and Wales, the book club is accessed via secure laptops. These allow prisoners to access preloaded reading materials and activities in their cells without requiring internet access, and offers an alternative to organised reading activities.

We designed guided reading and creative writing exercises at beginner, intermediate and advanced levels. Questions invite readers to explore characters’ decisions, consider different perspectives and develop their own interpretations. Creative exercises encourage them to imagine alternative storylines or draw connections with their own experiences, without requiring personal disclosure.

Read more:
Britain’s reading revival may be failing to reach those most disconnected from books

Participation is voluntary for prisoners. Those who complete and submit their activities can receive a University of Hull certificate, offering recognition that may be meaningful for people who lack confidence in their reading and writing abilities.

The aim is not simply to provide electronic texts, but to create opportunities for independent literary engagement, reflection and creative expression. Readers can participate privately, without the pressure of a classroom or group discussion.

Why contemporary books matter

Developing the digital book club also raised another question: what books could people actually read? Choice matters, and reading for pleasure involves discovering different authors, genres and stories, including contemporary literature.

We wanted to move beyond the titles already in the public domain. So we approached The Reading Agency with a proposal to make its Quick Reads titles – which were already available digitally through our existing book club – free to people in prison.

Unbeknown to us, the charity was already planning a major initiative to mark 20 years of Quick Reads. Nearly half a million copies of 11 titles were to be distributed across UK prisons, supported by author events, workshops and National Prison Radio activities. The programme also had the backing of author Lee Child, the UK’s first prison reading laureate.

Digital provision was not originally part of its plans, but The Reading Agency welcomed our proposal. As a result, four of the 11 Quick Reads in Prison titles are now available as ebooks, including one by Child, accompanied by our guided reading and creative writing activities.

This was made possible through the charity’s willingness to embrace the proposal and the agreement of authors and publishers to license their work for secure digital use.

What began as a University of Hull project has now become a new element of a national reading initiative, demonstrating how research, reading organisations and the publishing industry can work together to widen access to contemporary literature.

The next chapter belongs to publishers

The four Quick Reads titles have been licensed for digital access for just six months. This is an important start, but it raises a wider question: why should access to contemporary literature in prisons be exceptional rather than commonplace?

We believe that books should not be a privilege to be earned, or reading an opportunity dependent on institutional routines. People in prison should be able to discover and enjoy literature as part of everyday life.

Digital books can help make this possible. They cannot replace physical books, libraries, reading groups or author visits, nor should they. Each offers something different. But in-cell access can reach people who might otherwise struggle to participate, allowing them to read independently and at a time that suits them.

Now publishers now have an opportunity to build on this progress by making more titles available for secure digital use and supporting longer licensing periods.
Four titles and a six-month licence should be the beginning, not the limit of our ambition.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Accurate job descriptions and pay transparency shouldn’t be radical ideas
articles.summary:
Drazen Zigic/Shutterstock

Salary negotiations can feel like a bit of a game, but new UK legislation may change the rules. Under draft government plans, employers will be required to publish the salary range for any job advertised.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised a legal requirement for pay transparency in job adverts. There have also been proposals for equal pay reforms for those with disabilities or of an ethnic minority.

However, the Equality and Human Rights Commission is going further. It is urging governments to prevent employers from asking candidates about their existing salaries or expectations.

Recruitment is a game played on a very uneven playing field. Hiring the wrong recruit can be expensive and time consuming. But the toll placed on someone who finds themselves in the wrong job can be deep and enduring, potentially damaging their physical and mental health, work engagement, job satisfaction, and diminishing their confidence in their own abilities.

Employers have traditionally used previous earnings as a benchmark or indication of the salary a candidate would be prepared to accept. It’s also a proxy for their value – assuming that we are all worth what other people have decided to pay us.

From a potential employer’s perspective, a candidate’s high previous salary is understood as a sign of “latent quality”. This means it’s an indication of hidden abilities and skills that might not have been revealed at the interview.

Candidates can, of course, refuse to disclose their salary, but even that comes at a cost. It could give the impression that they are less skilled and have fewer alternative options. Gender stereotypes lead recruiters to believe that men are more comfortable discussing money, so they are viewed with more suspicion if reluctant to disclose their current earnings.

Questions about salary expectations can also be tricky for candidates to manage. Opt too low and you risk being offered a lower starting salary. Too high and you reduce your chances of a job offer. Evidence suggests that a collaborative approach and a precise starting bid seem to serve candidates well in their salary negotiations. For example, asking for £34,575 works better than £35,000.

Making salaries fairer for all

Much of the gender pay gap can be traced back to starting salaries. The explanations for this are complex, but include the anchoring effects of the salaries that recruiters expect to pay. This includes lower initial rates for female candidates, and the salaries that candidates feel able to ask for: men are more likely to negotiate hard when it comes to their starting salary, and employers are more likely to concede to their demands.

A similar story is seen with ethnicity. Certain groups – for example Black candidates and those from south-east and east Asia – seem to come out of negotiations with a worse deal. Racial and gender stereotypes can influence both candidates’ and recruiters’ behaviour.

The gender pay gap can be traced back to women being given lower starting salaries.
fizkes/Shutterstock

The current system of anchoring future salaries to previous salaries perpetuates discrimination, allowing people who hold privilege to cling on to an early advantage throughout their careers. Differences in starting salaries endure for years and it’s estimated that two thirds of the steady-state gender pay gap in the UK – meaning the wage gap that would occur if employment levels were constant and steady, rather than fluctuating as they do now – can be traced back to gender differences in starting salaries.

Furthermore, job adverts are not always an accurate reflection of what the role entails. They’re designed to sell the job to prospective employees. AI-curated job adverts are beginning to sound similar, making it ever harder for a candidate to work out whether they would actually like the job.

Typical AI-generated job adverts are often vague and are full of corporate buzzwords, leaving the potential candidate unsure about what the employer is looking for.

Job descriptions often reflect an idealised account of the role. They are generally written from the perspective of the employer rather than employee. For this reason, they can be light on the day-to-day realities.

Employers might offer interview candidates the chance to ask questions, but this is generally just an extension of the selection process. All parties are aware that this is not the time for an honest conversation.

Experiences vary, but candidates often have little more than a job advert and a single interview to go on. Ultimately this may well backfire for the employer. The organisation might find themselves with the “best” candidate on paper. But if they have missold the job, or misrepresented the organisation, it can lead to unrealistically high employee expectations, lower job satisfaction and a higher chance that their new recruit will quit their job.

“Realistic job previews”, where employers give an honest account of what the job is actually like, have been shown to have a positive impact on employers’ ability to recruit and retain good candidates. Studies have shown that when employees are invited to talk to candidates honestly about the job and the organisation, and are open about the challenges and stresses, potential recruits feel more positive about the integrity of the employer. Their expectations of the role are also more realistic, and they end up performing better and wanting to stay with the new organisation.

Staff turnover is an expensive business. Annual employee turnover across the UK is 34% on average. The cost of replacing each employee earning £25,000 or more is approximately £30,614 for the employer. Any improvements that can be made to the selection process to ensure that new hires are in it for the long haul could reap significant financial rewards.

The plans to increase transparency in salary negotiations feel like a step in the right direction, but providing an accurate description of the job shouldn’t be hailed as a radical approach. Job selection is the start of an ongoing relationship which is bound to be more successful if it starts with more transparency and collaboration.

Julia Yates does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: If politicians really want to cut heating bills they need to trust in green energy – businesses already are
articles.summary:
JustJus/Shutterstock

This year’s United Nations climate summit, Cop31, ended in Antalya without a deal.

It appears that the world’s politicians and policy makers have collectively moved on from building a global coalition against climate change, just as its effects are becoming impossible to ignore.

Yet the public have not stopped worrying. In a 2025 global Ipsos survey, 64% of adults said failing to act on climate change would hurt future generations.

And in 2026 around 60% of American adults think global efforts will not be enough to avoid the worst effects of climate change.

But perhaps the biggest hurdle to making more climate-friendly changes is the current cost-of-living crisis. It appears to be politically difficult to tell cash-strapped voters to be more environmentally friendly.

Opponents of policies tackling climate change, including British and European right-wing parties and Donald Trump, seem to have effectively persuaded a majority of the public that it is impossible to make climate-friendly choices and keep your bills down. In 2026, 62% of the UK public expected net zero – Britain’s route to climate neutrality – to increase their bills in the short run.

Read more:
Cop31: Why the UN climate summit ended in victory for fossil fuel producing nations

Voters often tend to overestimate how much they would lose from a carbon tax, and to underestimate how much others care.

But despite this, people are starting to notice that climate action cannot be blamed for an economic and environmental crisis fuelled by gas and petrol prices.

The 62% share of voters who think net zero increases their bills is the lowest on record. And 51% expect net zero to be good for the economy in the long run – only 24% think it will hurt it.

Politicians are right to be careful about what voters will accept. French president Emmanuel Macron has learned the hard way, after ten years of public protests, that taxing petrol is unpopular. In Milan, some voters owning polluting cars said they were likely to vote for the far right when the city banned their vehicles from the city centre.

But very few politicians make the point that the cost-of-living crisis would be much worse without green policy.

Cost-of-living crisis is a fossil fuel crisis

In 2021, Russia supplied around 40% of the EU’s pipeline gas imports. Scrambling to replace these imports with liquefied gas from Qatar and the US has sent energy prices through the roof.

Because of its past dependency on Russian fossil fuels, Europe now pays around ten times more than the US for the same quantity of gas. These high prices have hurt the economy and pushed up inflation.

Every unit of electricity generated by wind turbines, solar panels and nuclear power plants cuts consumer bills.

Those resources saved £5.9 billion in gas imports for the UK at the start of the Iran conflict when shipping was blocked through the Strait of Hormuz. Every time no gas is needed to produce electricity, prices come down.

Significant economic damage can be caused by ignoring this. It has been clear for some time now that the future is made of electric cars and batteries. Yet European carmakers still lobby for a perpetual delay of the transition.

This strategy is costing jobs today, having transformed Europe’s leading carmakers into global laggards.

And it also hurts consumers. The world’s cheapest electric cars are made in China. EU efforts to protect what remains of its car industry using tariffs mean they cost consumers 45% more.

Britain has so far avoided the extra cost. But the EU is pushing it to impose similar tariffs.

The largest wind farm in the world opened off the Grimsby coast in 2025.

Business is investing in green energy

But global investors are not as backward-looking as governments. This year, green energy investment is expected to reach US$2.2 trillion (£1.68 trillion) – almost double the investment in fossil fuels, and double the global investment in artificial intelligence. More than 90% of large-scale renewable investment in 2025 was cheaper than the cheapest fossil fuel alternative.

The same self-interested approach could apply to ordinary citizens.

An electric car costs less to run than a petrol one. But delays in the transition mean there are still too few charging points to make it practical for everyone.

Another factor is that in England, for instance, road congestion is taking an increasing toll on the economy, and this primarily affects motorists. Even in the US, where public transport accounts for less than 1% of journeys, when subways are not working, these few passengers switching to the car increase road congestion by 47%.

Pro-car lobbies do try to block investment in walkable cities and public transport. Will they take responsibility for the projected 85% increase in British road congestion by 2040?

Migration is very high on voters’ list of concerns, higher than any other in some British polls. And the consequences of climate change, such as flooding and high temperatures, are among the top reasons people leave their home countries. Without international cooperation on issues like water and energy, the flow of people wanting to escape poverty to live in less affected countries is likely to go up.

We live in an ageing world, and it appears that people are increasingly scared of change. The global mood feels protectionist and as crises accumulate, many want to put their own country first.

Very few environmental activists or politicians seem to speak to these instincts.

But green electricity makes you independent from foreign dictators, global cooperation should make migration more manageable, and many of our current problems come from ignoring climate change, not from trying to address it.

Renaud Foucart does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: We need to talk about young people’s sexual wellbeing – here’s why
articles.summary:
YesPhotographers/Shutterstock.com

Something is changing in Britain’s bedrooms. People in their late teens and early twenties are having sex later and less often than previous generations, and one in three 16- to 24-year-olds now say they have never had sex.

These are among the headline findings from the latest British National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4), the once-a-decade study that has tracked the nation’s sex lives since 1990. The latest survey, published across five papers in the Lancet, shows just how much has changed in young people’s sex lives in the last ten years.

At first glance, the headline finding could be seen as good news. Perhaps young people are taking more time before becoming sexually active and making decisions that feel right for them.

Yet alongside changes in sexual activity, Natsal-4 also found that young people had the lowest sexual wellbeing of any age group surveyed. At a time of life when sex is often assumed to be carefree, nearly one in four women aged 16-24, and almost one in five men of the same age, had low sexual wellbeing. Across all participants aged 16-59, the figure was closer to one in seven.

Sexual wellbeing is about much more than whether someone is having sex, or even whether that sex is enjoyable. It is about how people feel about this part of their lives. Do they feel comfortable and confident in themselves? Do they feel respected by others? Can they think or talk about sex without shame or embarrassment? Do they feel able to make choices that are right for them, and get support when they need it?

Sex and relationships are woven into many people’s sense of identity, connection with others, and overall wellbeing. Yet conversations about sex – particularly with young people – often focus on what can go wrong, rather than what helps people feel secure and at ease.

A young person might manage to avoid an unplanned pregnancy or a sexually transmitted infection, but still struggle with feelings of shame about sex. And concerns about sexual wellbeing are not limited to those who are sexually active. Young people who are not having sex may also experience pressures or worries.

The decline in sexual activity may matter less than whether young people feel comfortable and confident about their sex lives.

It’s not easy to say why this decline in sexual activity is happening. Young adults today face major economic pressures: insecure employment, high housing costs and delayed financial independence. There are fewer opportunities to meet and connect with others in-person, while social media and digital technologies have created new sources of social comparison, scrutiny and anxiety.

The COVID pandemic also disrupted a critical period of social and relationship development for many of today’s young people.

In the Natsal-4 survey, people with low sexual wellbeing were more likely to report symptoms of anxiety and depression, and this was particularly the case for men. This relationship almost certainly works in both directions. Poor mental health may make it harder to form or maintain intimate relationships, while worries about sex and intimacy may themselves contribute to emotional distress.

Although we cannot say what causes what, the findings reinforce a simple point: if we care about mental wellbeing, we need to care about sexual wellbeing too, as the evidence shows the two are so intimately intertwined.

COVID also disrupted young people’s relationships.
Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com

Different for women and men

Low sexual wellbeing is not experienced in the same way by everyone. While overall levels of low sexual wellbeing were similar in men and women of all age groups (one in seven), the patterns underlying them differed in important ways.

Women were more likely than men to report having someone they could talk to openly about their sex life. At the same time, they were more likely to report being upset with others about past sexual experiences.

Men, meanwhile, were more likely to report having a pleasurable sex life, but also more likely to feel shame about some of their thoughts and desires.

These differences reflect the distinct social pressures and expectations that continue to shape women’s and men’s experiences of sex and relationships. They also suggest that improving sexual wellbeing is unlikely to be as simple as increasing knowledge. It may also require enabling people to talk openly about insecurities and expectations in their sexual lives.

For years, public discussions about young people’s sexual lives have focused on whether they are having sex, at what age and how often. The latest Natsal findings suggest that we need to pay attention not only to what they do, but also to how they feel. For many young people, sexual wellbeing remains an overlooked part of the picture. It is time to start talking about it.

Correction: “males” and “females” has been changed to “men” and “women” to accurately reflect the terminology used in the survey.

Kirstin Mitchell receives funding from Scottish Government to research and embed sexual wellbeing in sexual health services nationally. The Natsal-4 study was funded by a grant from the Wellcome Trust with contributions from the UK ESRC and UK NIHR. Kirstin has received speaker fees from the College of Sexual and Relationships Therapists and travel reimbursement from the College of Sexual and Reproductive Health to talk on sexual wellbeing. In 2026, after the submission of the Natsal sexual wellbeing paper, Kirstin was an unpaid contributor to an educational series hosted by Reckitt (manufacturer of Durex condoms).

Ruth Lewis receives funding from Scottish Government to research and embed sexual wellbeing in sexual health services nationally.

articles.title: Strength training can help preserve muscle while using weight-loss drugs, research shows
articles.summary:
Zamrznuti tonovi/ Shutterstock

Weight-loss drugs are helping people to lose substantial amounts of weight and improve their health. However, this weight and body fat loss can also be accompanied by a loss of muscle and strength.

A new landmark study now shows that doing strength training while taking weight loss drugs can help.

Weight-loss drugs such as Mounjaro and Wegovy can have substantial health benefits. Alongside large reductions in body weight and body fat, they can also help people who are overweight and have heart disease to improve blood pressure, blood glucose and blood cholesterol levels, and lower the risk of having a heart attack or stroke.

However, as these drugs become more widely used, it’s important to consider whether solving one health problem could contribute to another.

The weight lost when taking these drugs includes some lean tissue – including muscle. There are several reasons for this.

Weight-loss drugs work by suppressing appetite and reducing food intake. When food intake falls, the body adapts to having fewer resources available and slows the production of new muscle.

Eating less food often means you’re consuming less protein overall. This means your body has less supply of the essential building blocks it needs to make new muscle. As body weight falls, every day movements place less load on the muscles which reduces the stimulus needed to maintain them.

Together, all of this leads to muscle loss. And this loss of muscle may have consequences for strength and independence.

Muscle strength helps you do everyday activities such as climbing the stairs, carrying shopping, getting out of a chair and steadying your body during a stumble.

The concern with weight-loss treatment is that substantial losses of muscle and strength could take people closer to a threshold below which they struggle to function independently and are at an increased risk of falls. This is of particular concern for older adults, since people already naturally tend to lose muscle and strength as we age.

Maintaining muscle

This recent trial involved 120 adults in Australia aged 50-70 years who were overweight or obese and did not exercise often. Everyone received the weight loss drug therapy (specifically tirzepatide – also known as Mounjaro) for 40 weeks.

The researchers then randomly assigned participants to either carry on with their usual levels of activity or do three strength training sessions each week. The training progressed slowly. Participants started with lighter exercises to learn the safe movements before increasing the challenge of performing each exercise. The sessions were also supervised by a qualified clinical exercise physiologist.

Both groups lost a large amount of weight (about 22kg on average) and body fat (about 17kg) during the 40-week period. They also saw similar improvements in their blood pressure, blood glucose and blood cholesterol levels.

The strength training group lost less muscle and built strength.
New Africa/ Shutterstock

Both groups lost some lean soft tissue (including muscle) but strength training offset some of this. The non-strength training group lost 4.7kg of lean tissue, while the strength training group only lost 3.6kg.

Strength was tested in both groups. The test involved straightening the knee against resistance (a knee extension exercise). People who just continued their normal activities could lift about 4kg less by the end of the study. But those who did the strength training throughout could lift 6kg more. The same pattern was found for two tests of upper body strength.

So despite losing some muscle, the exercise group got much stronger.

No specific dietary advice was given to the groups, other than to maintain protein intake. So this effect appears to be wholly down to the strength training.

The improvement in strength is probably explained by the strength training both preserving the amount of muscle and at the same time improving the quality of that muscle.

Strength training and weight loss

The study shows that doing strength training while taking a weight-loss drug can help people maintain muscle and improve strength.

For those who want to give strength training a try, aim to do two or three strength-focused sessions each week. Start with a light or moderate effort and build up gradually.

In the study, the first eight weeks were spent developing the correct technique and getting accustomed to exercise before the difficulty was gradually increased. Follow that principle by starting with manageable body weight exercises or using light resistance bands.

Build towards doing two sets of eight to 12 repetitions of each exercise, where the final couple of repetitions feel challenging. You should aim to do eight to ten different exercises in each session. Try to include lower body exercises (such as a body weight squat or a calf raise) and upper body exercises (such as a wall push up or a lat pull down using a resistance band). If eight to ten exercises per session feels daunting, then it’s fine to start with four to six exercises and build up over time. Be sure to pick exercises you enjoy doing.

As you get more confident and body weight exercises start to feel easier, you can gradually add more resistance. Just remember to keep good technique.

Strength training can help you maintain the muscle strength you need to move well and stay independent throughout ageing. These new findings further highlight the benefit it can have during weight-loss treatment by protecting muscle.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI is a huge cultural moment – it’s time to stop asking if video games are art
articles.summary:
On November 10 2026, PlayStation and Xbox owners across the UK began downloading a 212GB file. Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) would not come out until November 19, but the pre-load alone broke Virgin Media O2’s records for peak traffic and daily data volume.

In December 2023, GTA VI’s first trailer drew more than 93 million views in 24 hours, a YouTube record for a non-music video. In May 2025 the second trailer exceeded 475 million views in a day.

But one of the most telling signs of the game’s cross-cultural reach comes from basketball. On November 18, the eve of GTA VI’s release, the Miami Heat basketball team hosted the Milwaukee Bucks in a regular NBA game the club billed as “A Night in Vice City”.

Vice City is Grand Theft Auto’s fictional version of Miami, and for one night the Heat basketball team existed in that world. The players wore Vice City kit and fans were able to snack at Burger Shot and Cluckin’ Bell, the game’s fictional fast-food chains.

Between 2018 and 2021, the Heat’s “Vice” jerseys paid tribute to the 1980s TV drama Miami Vice. This time around the reference point is a video game. It is clear that video games are no longer simply covered by other culture – they are actively reshaping it.

This article is part of our State of the Arts series. These articles tackle the challenges of the arts and heritage industry – and celebrate the wins, too.

Read more:
Quality time and gifting flowers: why we love that GTA became a game about relationships

But it wasn’t always like this. In our forthcoming book, Consuming Video Games, fellow sociologist Tom Brock and I trace how video games began as experiments in military-funded research labs, then moved into bars and arcades alongside jukeboxes and pinball machines.

These were largely the haunts of young men, and jukeboxes and pinball carried an air of youthful rebellion as a form of leisure that felt distinct from adult respectability. Arcade games took that image with them when consoles and home computers brought them into living rooms and bedrooms. Parents, teachers and commentators dismissed them as a frivolous distraction, or simply a passing craze.

My colleagues and I argue that games have been held back by a particular stereotype of young, geeky, possibly toxic masculinity. That stereotype was not without foundation.

For decades, games were marketed mostly at boys and young men. Women who played, made or wrote about games sometimes faced abuse. This was most visible during the 2014 GamerGate campaign that saw an orchestrated barrage of online abuse against women in gaming. But the behaviour of a vocal minority came to stand in for the medium as a whole, and our research with women in the industry and in gaming communities suggests that while there is still work to do, the culture is far broader than the stereotype allows.

Read more:
Nearly a third of female gamers feel guilty about their hobby – new study

Yet the old image lingers. One survey from our research suggests people still place video games alongside reality TV, tattoos and shopping malls as having no cultural value at all.

Finding its own path

Shut out of respectable culture, gaming built its own. Players “copied and swapped game tapes, traded tips in playgrounds, and read magazines”, while specialist magazines and TV programmes taught people how to talk about games. Games are now played, but also watched, discussed, performed, collected, mourned and lived.

The scale is no longer in question. More than half of British adults play video games, yet popularity is not the same as respect.

Writing in the Guardian’s gaming culture newsletter, Pushing Buttons, Keith Stuart predicted that coverage of GTA VI would follow “a familiar pattern”, with reviewers admitting they haven’t played a game since Pac-Man, “in a way they never would while discussing any other art form”. Jamie Sefton, managing director of the northern games network Game Republic, said he remains baffled “as to why games are still not covered extensively in mainstream media”.

Much in the same way film came to be taken seriously as art, legitimacy rarely comes from inside a culture. It is granted by outsiders who already hold cultural authority: critics, curators, broadcasters and funders.

Read more:
How GTA 6 became a global phenomenon we can’t ignore

Even then, only certain games are seen as having artistic merit, usually smaller independent ones such as Journey (2012) or Disco Elysium (2019). Blockbusters such as Call of Duty (2003) rarely, if ever, are. This splits games into a handful of worthy games and the rest, which does little for the medium as a whole.

GTA VI sits firmly in “the rest”. It is loud, commercial, violent and controversial, the kind of game that cultural gatekeepers have learned to dismiss. But in August 2026, Netflix premiered the GTA VI preview where it recorded 31.1 million views in four days and ranked top of the platform’s English-language film chart. A few months later, an NBA team dipped into the world of Vice City. These are exactly the kind of “outsiders” that can shift how a medium is seen.

Film, television and pop music all made the journey from dismissed to respected, and it is tempting to ask when games will follow. But asking whether games are art is possibly the wrong question. What matters is the place they already hold in people’s lives – and that broadcasters, sports clubs and others outside gaming are starting to take note.

articles.title: The Hillsborough Law requires public servants to be honest – but what does honesty actually mean?
articles.summary:
A Hillsborough memorial at Anfield Stadium in Liverpool. 4kclips/Shutterstock

The Hillsborough disaster in 1989 ultimately claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans. In the weeks that followed, South Yorkshire Police reviewed its officers’ written accounts before passing them to the official inquiry.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel later found that 164 statements had been substantially changed. In 116 of them, comments critical of the force were removed or altered. In 2021, two former officers and the force’s solicitor were tried over those changes. The case collapsed. The judge ruled that the original inquiry wasn’t a statutory one, and the police had no legal duty of candour there.

The public office (accountability) bill, known as the Hillsborough law, currently in the House of Lords, is meant to close that gap. Covering up to 1.9 million public servants, it would require authorities and officials to act with “candour, transparency and frankness” towards inquiries and investigations. Breaching that duty with the aim of obstructing them would be a crime. The bill also creates a new offence of misleading the public, with a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

Honesty has been one of the seven principles of public life since 1995. Hillsborough shows what can happen when a moral duty may be ignored at little cost. But once honesty becomes a legal duty, someone has to decide what it requires. That’s much harder than it sounds.

Honesty is more than not lying

Research on public health communication shows that official messages can fall short of honesty without anyone telling a lie. They might use true statements to create a false impression, which is known as paltering. For example, they can leave out the size of a benefit or the harms, strip out uncertainty, or present risks in whatever form looks most persuasive.

Imagine a council official is asked at an inquiry whether they were warned that a block of flats was unsafe. They reply: “I never received a report saying the building was unsafe.” That may be strictly true. But suppose they had received several emails from residents and a fire officer raising concerns about the building’s fire doors. Nothing they said was false, yet the inquiry would come away with the wrong picture.

The Hillsborough statements fit the same pattern: the deception lay in what had been taken out.

The bill seems to accept this. Its test for “seriously improper” conduct refers to dishonesty “whether by means of falsehood, concealment, obfuscation or otherwise”. It says an “act” includes “an omission or a course of conduct”. And the duty of candour requires officials to correct “any errors or omissions” in what they have already told an inquiry.

As a result of campaigning by families of Hillsborough victims, a number of state-mandated investigations were held into the disaster.
Pete Stuart/Shutterstock

But the bill uses the word “dishonesty” without defining it. Nor does it say what counts as “misleading”. That’s important because the line is blurry.

Every statement leaves something out. The duty of candour asks officials to provide information that’s “relevant to the inquiry or investigation”, but someone still has to decide what’s relevant. Not every omission is a cover-up.

The problem grows when the evidence is incomplete or disputed. To show that someone misled others, a court needs something to compare their statement with. Should that be the truth as it later emerged, or the best understanding at the time? Early in a public health emergency, for example, officials often have to speak before the science is settled.

This is why the difference between misinformation and disinformation matters. Misinformation is false or misleading content shared without meaning to deceive, whereas disinformation is spread on purpose. An official may give an inaccurate account because they were wrongly briefed, or may not have realised a detail mattered. That’s a failure, but not necessarily dishonesty.

Can honesty really be enforced through the law?

The bill deals with this through what lawyers call the “mental element” of an offence. To be guilty of misleading the public, officials must “act with the intention of misleading the public” or be “reckless as to whether their act will do so”. They must also “know, or ought to know, that their act is seriously improper”.

An act is only seriously improper if it “involved dishonesty that was significant or repeated” on a matter of significant public concern, caused or risked harm, and departed significantly from proper conduct.

This leaves courts with a hard task. Proving intent means piecing together what an official knew and believed at the time. Omissions are especially hard to prove. A prosecutor must show that the official had the information, understood that it mattered and chose not to share it.

Draw these boundaries too narrowly and the selective editing seen after Hillsborough could slip through again, because every sentence left in was technically true. Draw them too vaguely and officials may say less, hedge everything and send every statement through lawyers.

Criminal law also has to be clear enough for people to know in advance what’s forbidden. Honesty is a tricky concept, so it’s likely the Hillsborough law will be difficult to enforce.

The Hillsborough law already accepts that dishonesty can mean “concealment” or “obfuscation”, not just “falsehood”. What it doesn’t yet do is say where honest selection ends and dishonest concealment begins. Peers still have a chance to fix this by defining “dishonesty” and “misleading” in the bill or its guidance.

For public servants bound by the law, there is a practical lesson. “Did I say anything false?” is the wrong question. A better one is: “Will the people I’m speaking to come away with an accurate picture?”

Byron Hyde previously received funding from the Wellcome Trust to investigate the seven principles of public life.

articles.title: Climate diplomacy is stuck – these three big changes would get it moving again
articles.summary:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, held in Antalya, Turkey, was being branded “possibly the worst Cop in history” even before its sorry conclusion.

I was there, and the conference was badly managed from start to finish: initial traffic jams and queues sapped energy and goodwill, while the final plenary was one embarrassment after another, with the summit president sniping at the UN’s climate chief (to audible gasps from delegates), and the closing “Antalya pact” being comprehensively rejected.

This sad outcome was not merely the fault of the conference’s Turkish-Australian presidency, however. The bigger issue is that climate diplomacy is stuck – and has been for several years. Structural changes are required, three in particular.

1. Climate finance is not an optional extra

First, climate finance – money provided to developing countries to help them tackle climate change – has to be increased, in particular public, grant-based finance from developed states.

This may seem an odd place to start for those weaned on the mainstream western media, where most accounts of Cop31’s failure focused on the stand off over fossil fuels. But climate finance is not an optional extra under the Paris agreement: it is the glue that holds the entire arrangement together. Ensuring adequate finance flows is one of the agreement’s three main stated aims (alongside limiting global temperature rises and supporting adaptation). And these flows are meant to progressively increase in line with mitigation ambitions and adaptation needs.

But in recent years they have not. At Cop29 in Baku, an ambitious new finance goal was planned. But instead, the conference saw a pushed-through decision that failed to offer the “progression beyond previous efforts” required by Paris and drew widespread condemnation from developing states. Nigeria termed the deal “an insult” to the UN Climate Convention.

Actual country pledges and disbursements have been falling short too. This year has seen a 70% drop in total developed country finance pledges. Meanwhile, the UK is cutting its development assistance to 0.3% of gross national income, while halving its climate finance.

The consequences have been profound. By no coincidence, within a year of the finance debacle in Baku the other side of the global climate bargain had unravelled too. The 2025 round of national mitigation plans were barely more ambitious than their previous iterations, mostly late, and collectively non-compliant with the goals of the Paris agreement.

For many developing countries, inadequate climate finance was one of the biggest frustrations at Cop31.
Rehman Asad / Shutterstock

Cop31 continued this pattern. On the conference’s eve, EU Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra declared the prospects for additional climate finance “dead in the water”. New developed world pledges for the Adaptation Fund, which helps countries prepare for and cope with the effects of climate change, totalled just US$50 million, less than half the cost of a single F-35 fighter jet.

The predictable result was deadlock on most key negotiation tracks. Indeed, for many developing countries, as well as NGOs, it was above all this climate finance issue – and not the question of whether “fossil fuels” should be named or not – that most underpinned their rejection of the Antalya pact.

The lesson should be clear: to unblock future climate summits, vastly improved finance offerings will be needed from developed countries. And that means that money will have to be diverted from elsewhere, including from the US$2.9 trillion being spent globally on militaries and war.

2. Climate coalitions need to become alliances

More money will not be enough though. Sharper political strategies are also needed, ones that are appropriate to a geopolitically fractured world and to tackling fossil fuel interests.

Cop30 in Belém, Brazil, brought a big step forward on this, with its recognition that “coalitions of the willing” are needed to overcome the UN’s consensus rules. Right now, these rules effectively give fossil fuel-dependent countries a veto on meaningful action. This led to a new process explicitly focused on “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, which began with a 57-country summit in Santa Marta, Colombia, in early 2026.

The risk, though, is that such coalitions just become new talking shops, and lack teeth. The “national roadmaps” that countries in the Santa Marta coalition are producing seem to illustrate this: the first wave of published roadmaps contains not a single new major policy commitment.

But other coalitions show us what might be possible. On the greenhouse gas methane (the focus of my current research), a powerful network of international partnerships, NGOs, funders and regulatory initiatives has transformed policy and practice over the last five years.

And building on the EU’s world-leading methane regulation, this coalition is now constructing a global marketplace that rewards cleaner producers with preferential market access, in order to help drive down methane emissions.

To really work, however, both this and other such coalitions will need commitment, regulation and enforcement. Voluntary initiatives will not be enough. And over time, such ad hoc “climate clubs” will need to transform into something much firmer – binding, treaty-based climate alliances.

3. Public pressure and protest matter

Last, it should be stressed that progress in international climate politics is not the responsibility of diplomats alone. Whatever they achieve, or do not, always reflects diverse lobbying and social pressures.

And sadly, on this front there has been a sharp regression. Since a peak in 2020, mass climate activism has largely died out. Media coverage of climate change has declined worldwide. And, spurred on by the Trump administration and war, fossil fuel interests are ascendant.

These things will only be changed through education, mobilisation and a widespread taking to the streets.

As Tasneem Essop, executive director of the NGO Climate Action Network, put it during an early Cop31 press conference: “We cannot give up on multilateralism … But if we can’t win back home, we cannot expect to win things in this space.”

Jan Selby receives funding from the European Research Council. He is a member of the Green Party of England and Wales.

articles.title: The efficiency paradox: why greener AI means more waste
articles.summary:
Data centres are getting bigger and more abundant, not necessarily more efficient. cflaten/Shutterstock

AI is increasingly being promoted as a solution to climate change. It can help companies use less fuel, reduce waste and make production more efficient.

For example, AI can help delivery companies plan more efficient routes, reducing the fuel they use and the emissions they produce. Similar savings could be made across other industries and transport networks, potentially reducing the overall environmental impact. But greater efficiency can also encourage more consumption.

AI is being promoted as a climate solution and as a driver of competitiveness, productivity and economic growth. The World Trade Organization estimates that the widespread adoption of AI could increase global trade by around 40% by 2040. This is generally presented as a benefit.

But there is an obvious contradiction here. If AI makes firms more efficient and profitable, it encourages further investment and expansion. Successful firms do not use productivity gains to produce less, but to expand and to make greater profits.

When these dynamics are generalised across the economy, the result is more production, transportation, resource extraction, consumption and ultimately more environmental destruction.

This is capitalism’s efficiency paradox, known as the Jevons paradox. According to William Stanley Jevons, a 19th-century English economist, any increase in resource efficiency generates an increase in long-term resource consumption, rather than a decrease.

Read more:
DeepSeek claims to have cured AI’s environmental headache. The Jevons paradox suggests it might make things worse

New technologies can help businesses produce more goods using less energy, materials and labour. But by making production cheaper and faster, they can also encourage businesses to make and sell more, increasing the total amount of resources that people use.

Industrial efficiency gains have been a defining feature of capitalism since the Industrial Revolution. Steam-powered textile mills and coal mines in the late 18th century, the Bessemer steel process (making steel by blowing air through molten iron) in the 19th century, and Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th all dramatically increased efficiency.

The industrial revolution has evolved as efficiency improved, from the development of coal mines in the 18th century to Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th century.
Parilov/Shutterstock

Yet none of these efficiency gains reduced society’s overall consumption of resources. Rather, they underpinned successive waves of industrial expansion, fossil-fuel use and environmental degradation.

AI is no different.

My research shows how digital technologies provide a historical example of this dynamic.

For decades, improvements in computers, telecommunications and data storage have allowed companies to spread different stages of production across several countries. They can now use real-time digital networks to share information and coordinate manufacturing and trade around the world.

These technologies have made possible today’s highly integrated global supply chains, allowing firms to source components from thousands of suppliers and move goods across continents with extraordinary speed and precision.

The environmental consequences are immense.

Digital technologies have helped companies produce and sell more goods around the world. This has increased the demand for raw materials, pollution from transport and damage to the natural environment. International trade in goods is now linked to around 30% of threats to the world’s species

Rather than reversing these trends, AI is deepening them. It is making supply chains faster, more responsive and more geographically extensive. From a business perspective, this is progress. Environmentally, it accelerates ecological breakdown.

Cleaner technology, more fossil fuels

The same contradiction can be seen in the energy sector. Much discussion of AI and green technology assumes that cleaner technologies replace dirtier ones. Yet, as the historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz shows, new energy systems tend to accumulate on top of rather than substitute for each other.

Wood, coal, oil, gas and renewables have largely been added to one another rather than replacing one another. Green technologies are making fossil-fuel industries more efficient, rather than replacing them.

Many of the technologies being promoted as climate solutions, including AI, are actually accelerating the extraction of fossil fuels that is driving climate change.

In Guyana, since commercial oil production began in 2019, the country has become one of the world’s fastest-growing producers of oil, with targets to produce 1.3 million barrels per day by 2027. AI-enabled drilling and “geosteering” – the real-time adjustment of a well’s path to keep it within oil-bearing rock – are increasing the rate of oil extraction.

So, can a technology designed to increase productivity, competitiveness and growth solve a crisis rooted in relentless profit-oriented expansion of production and consumption on a finite planet? Until that question is confronted, greener AI is likely to make ecological destruction more efficient rather than bring it to an end.

Benjamin Selwyn works for the University of Sussex.

articles.title: Recruiting new trustees for The Conversation UK
articles.summary:
The Conversation Trust UK is the charity which operates the UK edition of The Conversation. Its Board of Trustees has overall responsibility for the charity, setting its strategy and overseeing its operations. The Board is chaired by Professor Paul Boyle, Vice-Chancellor of Swansea University. As several of our Trustees reach the end of their terms over the next 12 months, we are looking for new Trustees to join the board.

Role specification

As a Trustee you will work closely with fellow trustees and staff to make important decisions about The Conversation’s operations and strategy, and advise and support our team in doing the best work possible. It meets 4-5 times per year, both in person and virtually. Some Trustees also serve on subcommittees which meet between Board meetings, and all are encouraged to represent the charity externally. The Trustees are also supported by The Conversation’s Editorial Board.

We welcome expressions of interest from anyone who shares our commitment to the democratisation of knowledge and public engagement with research.

Trustees are asked to commit to a three year term, which can be extended for a further three year period by mutual agreement. Most trustees step down at the end of six years on the board.

Given The Conversation’s vision to be an inclusive and diverse organisation, including among our staff and contributors, we would welcome applications from under-represented groups, particularly people from Black, Asian or other minority ethnic backgrounds. We welcome applications from everyone regardless of age, gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation, faith or disability. All appointments will be made on merit, following a fair and transparent process. In line with the Equality Act 2010, however, The Conversation may employ positive action where diverse candidates can demonstrate their ability to perform the role equally well.

Application

To apply, please send a CV and brief supporting statement explaining your interest and relevant skills and experience to: uk-jobs@theconversation.com

If you would like an informal discussion about trusteeship, The Conversation or need further information, please contact Imogen Clark on uk-admin@theconversation.com to arrange a time to speak with the Editor or Chief Executive.

articles.title: Eminem and Damien Hirst collaboration shows the relationship between art and music is alive and well
articles.summary:
Few of even Eminem’s staunchest fans would have expected the rapper to find a home in a fine art gallery. Yet in 2026, when truth is often stranger than fiction, what was once inconceivable became a reality.

American Dream was a collaboration between the rapper and the artist Damien Hirst consisting of paintings and installations inspired by Eminem’s album covers. It was recently on display at London’s HENI gallery.

For centuries, western tradition has placed the visual arts at the top of an intellectual ladder, treating sight and sound as separate domains. Today however, artists, curators and researchers are increasingly interested in how our senses of sight and sound overlap, interact and enrich one another.

As a researcher of music, I find the combination of visual art and music to be one of the most fascinating pairings. At their core, the two art forms may be distinct forms of human expression, but they are deeply connected by how their use of space, rhythm and movement can express emotional responses and experiences for their viewers, listeners, or even the creators themselves.

Indeed, the two go together so well that they can be found sitting together on millions of shelves in millions of homes all over the world.

Ever since 1938, when graphic designer Alex Steinweiss created the first illustrated 78rpm record album cover (Smash Song Hits by Rodgers & Hart, which featured the songwriters’ names in lights on a shimmering marquee) popular music and visual art have been inseparable.

In his 2008 book A Brief History of Album Covers, author Jason Draper observed that some album covers are genuine pieces of high-class art that should be revered as much as the music. He cites The Beatles’ Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, Sex Pistols’ Never Mind the Bollocks and Cindi Lauper’s She’s So Unusual as examples.

Perhaps due to its ability to reach vast audiences, the medium has appealed to several revered visual artists over the years. Andy Warhol, Peter Blake, Banksy and Takashi Murakami have all created cover art across a range of musical genres.

In my new book Reading Eminem, I explain that the album format has always been Eminem’s primary form of expression. The artwork found on his front and back covers, booklets and tray inserts has been a significant part of that.

From the grotesque cartoon imagery of 1999’s The Slim Shady LP through to the “body bag” image on 2024’s The Death of Slim Shady (Coup de Grâce), Eminem has used visuals art as a way to enhance the stories and characters contained within the songs themselves.

With 2004’s Encore CD booklet photographs, Eminem has even provided fans with an additional narrative, appearing to shoot at his audience at the end of a performance.

Album art in galleries

In recent years, the humble album cover has even been deemed worthy of promotion to art gallery status. Exhibitions such as For the Record: Photography & the Art of the Album Cover at The Photographers’ Gallery, London, Art & Vinyl at Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco and Playback: Art Of The Album Sleeve at Lincoln Castle have underscored the medium as a serious artform.

In 2022, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art collaborated with Interscope, commemorating the label’s 30th anniversary by displaying reinterpretations of Interscope album art from an intergenerational group of visual artists. Among them was Hirst, who re-imagined album covers from Eminem’s discography based on their themes and lyricism.

Described by the HENI gallery as “a landmark collaboration that unites two of the most influential forces in contemporary art and music”, the show American Dream combined Hirst’s trippy interpretations of 12 Eminem album covers with a series of pharmaceutical-themed installations and visual motifs inspired by the rapper’s lyrics.

On the face of it, the exhibition may not have offered anything ground-breaking. But the fact that album covers, once considered part of a “low” culture medium, are being displayed in settings previously reserved for highbrow cultural capital is significant. I for one hope this trend continues.
