Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com

Described as the “Ferrari of the virus world” for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

Reports from the UK Health Security Agency have highlighted that cases of norovirus – commonly known as the “winter vomiting bug” – have increased by more than 35% in England over the past two weeks, compared with the previous fortnight.

While that sounds alarming, this is still within expected levels for the season. Overall case numbers are about 5% above what’s typical for this time of year. Cases have fallen in Scotland, but Wales has seen a rise.

Norovirus symptoms include sudden-onset nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, sometimes accompanied by fever, stomach pain, body aches and headaches.

Most healthy adults recover within one to three days. However, those with weakened immune systems, older adults and young children face a higher risk of severe symptoms. When this happens, people can be ill for much longer and may need hospital treatment if they become dehydrated.

Norovirus is highly contagious, with some studies suggesting that as few as ten virus particles can cause an infection. It spreads from person to person when tiny amounts of virus from infected faeces or vomit get on to food, hands or surfaces and are then transferred to the mouth.

Close contact between people can also spread the virus. This may help explain why cases peak in winter, when people spend more time together indoors. However, you can catch it at any time of the year.

The virus is also particularly resilient; it can survive on hard kitchen surfaces such as stainless steel and ceramic for up to two weeks, and it takes temperatures of around 60°C to kill it.

There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for norovirus. It evolves quickly to escape our immune systems, and has proved notoriously difficult to grow in the lab, which has hampered research efforts. That said, recent breakthroughs in growing norovirus using lab-grown human gut cells may make it easier to develop treatments in future.

How to protect yourself and your household

While alcohol-based hand sanitisers can be effective against other viruses, such as the ones that cause COVID and flu, they don’t work well against norovirus. Instead, the best way to protect yourself is by washing your hands often with soap and hot water, ideally for 15 seconds or more. This is particularly important before or after preparing food, and after going to the toilet.

Norovirus is also frequently spread through contaminated food. Fresh produce such as fruit and vegetables may pick up the virus during harvesting, packaging or handling, so wash these thoroughly before use. Shellfish such as oysters can also be contaminated with concentrated norovirus from the water they live in, so ensure these are thoroughly cooked, rather than steamed or eaten raw.

If someone in your household has norovirus, cleaning surfaces regularly with bleach-based products can help prevent the virus from spreading.

Using a dummy called Vomiting Larry, researchers found that norovirus-containing droplets can spread around ten feet (three metres) when someone vomits. So, it’s important to immediately clean areas that have been contaminated by vomit or faeces.

Vomiting Larry in action.

Frequent cleaning of heavily used surfaces such as door handles, light switches, taps, toilet seats and flush handles, ideally while wearing disposable gloves, can help reduce the chances of the virus spreading.

Washing soiled clothes or bedding separately from other laundry, at a temperature of 60°C or above at the longest cycle time possible, can also help kill the virus on soft surfaces.

If you are unlucky enough to get norovirus yourself, the only solution is to allow the virus to run its short, but deeply unpleasant, course.

Replacing lost fluids is essential, so drink plenty of water, tea or electrolyte drinks, or use oral rehydration sachets. If you feel able to eat, stick to plain foods that are easy to digest, such as toast, rice, pasta or soup, and avoid fatty or salty foods that may make your symptoms worse.

As norovirus is highly contagious, ensure that you stay at home and rest as much as possible. Keep your distance from other people in your household where you can, and avoid preparing food for others while you’re unwell and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.

Even after full recovery, infectious virus can still be shed in poo for up to two weeks, so continuing to frequently clean bathroom areas can help prevent further transmission.

With cases rising as winter sets in, the Ferrari of viruses may be doing the rounds for a while yet. A few simple habits could save you, and others, a very unpleasant few days.

Charlotte Lewis receives funding from the UK Medical Research Council.

articles.title: Joanne Young waived her anonymity – my research shows why survivors of sexual violence make this brave choice
articles.summary:
Echoing the case of Gisèle Pelicot in France, Joanne Young waived her right to anonymity following the conviction of her ex-husband for drugging her, raping her and allowing other men to rape her too. Philip Young had routinely drugged his wife over many years, soliciting men online to come into their home and rape her.

In the UK and Ireland, victims of sexual violence are entitled to lifelong anonymity. This reflects an enduring reality: rape and sexual assault remain highly stigmatising experiences.

Yet there is growing evidence that survivors are choosing to forgo that protection. Along with colleagues, I have been systematically studying those who choose to waive their right to anonymity. Though survivors’ experiences are very different, common themes emerge.

By waiving this right, Young and Pelicot have opened up a conversation about violence against women and girls. This conversation is sorely needed.

During their trial, Norman Macksoni, Richard Wilkins, Connor Sanderson-Doyle and Mohammed Hassan argued that their sexual activity with the unconscious Joanne Young was consensual as her then-husband gave consent. Another man, Dean Hamilton, admitted charges including rape in February, and Philip Young also pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing to a string of offences.

Pelicot and supporters of Young have said that shame must change sides. They are not wrong. In the UK case, here is a cohort of men who argued in open court that a husband has the power to decide who has sexual access to his wife. That is both shocking and shameful.

Agency and empowerment

Victims of sexual assault experience domination of their bodily autonomy in the most intimate way. And they often describe their experiences in court as similarly intrusive and violating. Intimate videos are replayed, there can be extensive scrutiny of their sexual history and relentless questions about their consent.

Reasserting their agency is another key motivation of those who waive their anonymity. Speaking can be empowering after a trial where they have had very little control over the outcome. In the all too rare instances when a conviction is secured (unlike when it is not), victims are free to speak. Those who feel they have survived both the abuse and the judicial system often feel compelled to speak on behalf of the many others who don’t seek or get justice.

There is a final reason that survivors can be motivated to waive their anonymity. Doing so can allow them to find solidarity with others who share their experience. Sexual violence is associated with a high burden of ill health compared to other traumatic life events. This might be mental health consequences including depression and post-traumatic stress, and physical issues including cardiovascular, metabolic and immune disorders.

Going public can allow survivors to find solidarity with others.
Steve Travelguide/Shutterstock

Research consistently shows that deliberate, intentional acts of violence disproportionately damage people’s faith in others. This can make it difficult for victims to connect with others. This is amplified in cases where the perpetrator is a family member. Previously trusted husbands and fathers have not only exploited their position in the family unit, they have fractured relationships.

For many, and particularly for women where family roles are heavily emphasised, much of their identity is defined by these relationships: daughter, wife or mother. Alongside shame, sexual abuse corrupts these identity-based relationships, further disconnecting victims when they need support.

Philip Young, a former Conservative councillor in Swindon, Wiltshire, harnessed the power of like-minded others. At short notice, after he had drugged Joanne, he was able to find ample men in a small geographical area willing to assault his unconscious wife.

In going public, Young and Pelicot have both harnessed the power of like-minded others for good. Waiving anonymity can allow victims to connect with others at a very vulnerable point in their lives.

But Lavinia Kerwick, the first woman in Ireland to waive her anonymity after the conviction of her rapist in 1991, has described the burden of doing so. The survivor rather than the perpetrator becomes publicly synonymous with the crime. It can become a lens through which others see victims.

Waiving anonymity is not for everyone and certainly shouldn’t be an expectation placed on survivors. And clearly survivors make their decisions based on their own circumstances and concerns. Either way, it is a difficult decision.

Survivors are acutely aware that waiving anonymity comes at a personal cost. But for those who do, their actions are driven by collective rather than personal concerns. In research with colleagues, we have referred to this phenomenon as collective post-traumatic growth. After their trauma, survivors rebuild a view of the world that includes the need for a different future, a better one for all. Drawing strength from the support and solidarity after their disclosure, they are driven to act on behalf of others.

Sexual violence is not simply a private, personal matter. It is a corrosive social force, the effects of which extend far beyond the family home. It damages relationships and communities, and shatters the integrity of our social, judicial and political institutions. Young, Pelicot and others waive their anonymity to progress social, political and legislative change for everyone. It’s time to trade in the shame and offer them our gratitude.

Orla Muldoon has received funding from the European Research Council.

articles.title: Swimming spots won’t get official bathing water status if they’re tricky to clean under England’s new rules
articles.summary:
Church Cliff beach, Lyme Regis, Dorset. Sarah2/Shutterstock

If a beach or riverside spot in England is popular with swimmers, anyone can apply for it to be given official bathing status. Official status means that the water will be tested and monitored regularly, and given a rating from “excellent” to “poor”.

Now, though, popular swimming spots can be refused official bathing water status in England if government agencies judge that meeting minimum water quality standards will be too difficult or disproportionately expensive.

Until recently, official bathing status was granted to a place being used by large numbers of swimmers – the water did not have to be clean before designation. A site could be granted official bathing status while being classified as “poor”, with recommendations to avoid swimming there. Bathing status designation and water quality classification were separate.

But official status requires regular Environment Agency testing for bacteria that indicate faecal contamination, with up to 20 samples taken during the bathing season, from May to September. Further requirements include information for swimmers and duties to investigate and address pollution.

England’s new rules, in force since May 2026, have added a check before official designation. Can water realistically be improved to at least “sufficient” status without disproportionate expense? A polluted site can still be designated if it passes that assessment, but designation must be refused if ministers accept that improvement is not feasible or is considered too expensive.

If status is refused by the Environment Agency (with final decisions being made by Defra, the government’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs), who will tackle the water pollution and keep swimmers informed?

Designation driving improvement

Church Cliff beach in Lyme Regis, Dorset, was first designated as a bathing water in 1988. Its water was classified as “poor” in 2015. Routine testing for bacteria in water stopped when the beach lost its official status in 2016 due to so few people swimming there.

But some people did continue to swim at Church Cliff beach. For two years, campaigners fought to restore its designation as an official bathing spot and secure action on pollution. The town council supported the public call for redesignation and subsequent water quality monitoring. People were still swimming at this beach and when designation returned in 2024, testing for bacteria resumed and pollution information signs followed. But the water had not been cleaned up in the interim and this site was classified as “poor” again that year.

Designation could help drive the work needed to help clean up water pollution. After redesignation of Church Cliff beach, the Environment Agency drew up a plan in 2025 to reduce sewage discharges, fix leaking pipes and tackle farm pollution. Utility company South West Water committed to sewage upgrades, while the town council worked with the Environment Agency to set up a group to oversee improvements.

For new applications, this process will not be possible if it is judged that improving water quality is not feasible or would be disproportionately expensive.

The government argues that limited resources should go where they can deliver results. It also wants to avoid giving swimmers false reassurance about places that cannot meet minimum standards. Yet Defra’s original 2024 consultation on reforming bathing water regulations acknowledged that refusing designation could discourage investment at polluted sites. Whether that happens will depend on how decisions are made and what follows.

These decisions depend on understanding pollution sources. At East Looe in Cornwall, the bathing water was rated “poor” in 2015. After heavy rain, the River Looe can carry runoff from farmland and sewage from overflowing sewers miles downstream to the beach.

Different sources call for different measures. Upstream in Liskeard, South West Water built two underground tanks to store wastewater during storms and reduce sewage spills into Looe Bay. This was part of a bathing water scheme completed in spring 2015. Cornwall Wildlife Trust offered farmers grants for better roofing and drainage to keep farm waste out of streams during heavy rain. In 2019, East Looe’s bathing water earned its first “good” rating, which it still held in 2025.

East Looe, Cornwall.
BijM/Shutterstock

The new rules under scrutiny

The new bathing water status application process includes water quality checks before designation and, where necessary, an assessment of whether improvements are feasible. But the published guidance does not specify how thoroughly each pollution source will be investigated.

The watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection welcomed the reforms. It has also called for clear reasons and public involvement.

Defra’s guidance on bathing water applications says decisions will be explained. Details of the feasibility assessment will follow. It remains unclear whether the method will follow the watchdog’s advice on calculating cleanup costs.

The environmental campaign charity Surfers Against Sewage is challenging the rules in court. Surfers Against Sewage argues that the new rules undermine the protections that designation is meant to provide. The High Court granted permission for the challenge to proceed in October 2026, with a hearing scheduled for February 2027.

Any refusal should explain which pollution sources were investigated, why cleanup was judged infeasible or too expensive, and what could allow reconsideration. It should clarify which monitoring will continue and who will inform swimmers. This would help people make informed choices and communities track whether pollution is being tackled.

For swimmers and river users, the consequences go far beyond a place on an official list. Without clear warnings, people may unknowingly enter polluted water and develop infections. These can cause diarrhoea and vomiting and, in severe cases, life-threatening complications such as kidney failure. Refusal should never mean abandoning efforts to improve water quality.

Karolina Krupska is the founder of the Water Science Foundation.

articles.title: What is resilience? It may be less about bouncing back than we think
articles.summary:
Halfpoint/Shutterstock

Resilience can sound empowering. Yet it can also become a responsibility, a socially imposed burden that people are expected to demonstrate when they are ill, ageing or struggling.

We are often told to be resilient. Mental health guidance, the media and even governments encourage us to become more resilient, as though resilience is something that we can build up and draw upon when life becomes difficult.

But resilience is not a superpower possessed by a fortunate few, nor simply a predetermined psychological resource that people carry with them. Rather, it is constituted through the relationships, routines, past experiences and opportunities to adapt. We don’t do it alone.

This matters because social conditions can make adapting to adversity easier or harder. Secure work, supportive relationships, accessible healthcare and financial resources can make it easier to to cope. Insecurity, isolation, poor health and limited alternatives can constrain our capacity to adapt.

In our research we followed people aged over 50 living with long COVID through three interviews conducted over 18 months. Their accounts take us beyond the popular idea of resilience as “bouncing back”. Instead, they show resilience being continually negotiated through relationships, external resources and wider social circumstances, as people navigate what has changed, what remains possible and what future they can imagine.

Caroline, 52, worked as a care worker on a zero-hours contract while living with persistent fatigue and brain fog, with little room to slow down or stop. She said, without work, “I don’t get any money”. She described taking only “a couple of minutes’ breather between each job” before carrying on.

She also felt pressure to appear as though she was coping: “I have to pretend that I’m alright, and then of course when I come home, it’s when I’m not.”

From a distance, this might look like resilience. But Caroline’s determination to keep going was shaped by financial insecurity and limited alternatives. Her capacity to adapt cannot be separated from the conditions in which she was trying to do so.

When resilience becomes an individual responsibility, people may feel pressured to pretend they are coping rather than seek support. This expectation to be resilient can itself become another burden.

Long Covid made these pressures particularly visible for the participants in our study. Its fluctuating symptoms could make it difficult to know whether changing capacities reflected illness, ageing or both. For people in their 50s and 60s, this could create a feeling of ageing “too soon”, while older participants sometimes faced assumptions that declining health was part of getting older.

Elizabeth, in her early 50s, described feeling trapped in a body that seemed much older than her age. Although others saw her as “back to normal”, she continued to struggle. There was, she said, “a bit of a gap between how people perceive you and how you’re feeling yourself”. Eventually, she described having to “fake it to make it”.

Her experience shows that resilience is not only shaped by material circumstances, but also by how other people understand us. Expectations about what someone of a particular age should be able to do can influence how they understand their own limitations.

Caroline and Elizabeth’s experiences remind us that when resilience becomes an individuality responsibility, it can lose its positive meaning.

These experiences challenge the idea that resilience is something innate we either have or lack. Instead, it is continually negotiated.

One way to imagine this is that resilience is less like armour and more like an immune system. Armour protects us by keeping adversity out. An immune system responds to what it encounters, interacting with its surrounding environment and continually adjusting. Similarly, social conditions make resilience possible.

Think of resilience as an immune system.
PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Kenneth, 61, was depressed in his first interview with us after losing work and hobbies. By the second, he had started a full-time job with a local council.

“Getting out and meeting people is great and feeling useful is great,” he said, linking his recovery closely to work and community participation: “If I was to draw a graph [of recovery and work], they would be very closely correlated.”

Arnold, 73, told us he experienced brain fog, vision loss and cardiac symptoms from long Covid, alongside the effects of a stroke more than ten years earlier. This left him reliant on his wife for many things. He described how he and his wife coped together: “we live for today”.

Yet when his wife died during the study, this shared way of coping was disrupted. His world became much smaller. His focus increasingly centred on simply getting through each day.

Kenneth and Arnold’s experiences show how resilience is not a fixed state, but something that can be strengthened, disrupted and reworked over time.

This matters beyond long Covid and ageing. Life brings uncertainties that cannot always be overcome; ill health, bereavement, changing relationships and shifting ideas about the future. Resilience may involve renegotiating who we are and what a good life might look like as these changes unfold.

It can mean adapting. It can mean accepting help. It can mean relinquishing an earlier version of ourselves.

Telling people to “be resilient” can obscure the conditions that make coping possible, including secure work, supportive relationships, accessible healthcare and financial resources.

Our research shows that resilience is an ongoing, often fragile way of living with uncertainty.

Chao Fang receives funding from NIHR (COV-LT-0009).

Alastair Comery receives funding from NIHR (COV-LT-0009).

articles.title: Pimple-popping videos can be disgusting – and strangely satisfying
articles.summary:
Pimple-popping videos leave some viewers squirming and others waiting eagerly for the next squeeze. Lena May/Shutterstock

Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger’s face. I’m one of them. I have favourite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

I tend to watch with the sound off and the speed doubled, slowing things down if a particularly promising spot needs closer attention. My hairdresser discovered this interest when she caught sight of my phone. She was considerably less enthusiastic.

But why does something that makes one person recoil keep another watching? And are people like me less easily disgusted in the first place?

In the latest episode of Strange Health, The Conversation’s podcast about unusual health and wellness trends, I explore pimple popping with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

Our guest is Albert Wabnegger, a scientist at the University of Graz in Austria who specialises in the psychology of disgust. He doesn’t particularly enjoy pimple-popping videos himself, but has spent rather more time studying them than most non-fans would volunteer for.

Measuring the pleasure of a popped pimple

Wabnegger and his colleagues developed a questionnaire to measure how much people enjoy popping their own spots or watching someone else’s being squeezed. He takes me through it during the episode. I rapidly develop concerns that the scale doesn’t go high enough.

For a study involving 80 women, the researchers showed enthusiasts and non-enthusiasts pimple-popping videos inside a brain scanner. For comparison, they showed water spraying from fountains and steam cleaners removing dirt from cars and stone floors.

Fans of pimple-popping videos reported more pleasure and less disgust while watching, although they still felt some disgust. On a separate questionnaire, the two groups gave similar ratings when asked how disgusting they found situations that might expose them to germs. Fans did report fewer difficulties managing feelings of disgust. The scans also revealed differences in activity in a brain region involved in motivation and reward.

Wabnegger explains why that needs careful interpretation. Brain activity cannot tell researchers precisely what somebody feels, and these findings don’t demonstrate a dopamine rush.

Enjoying disgust from a safe distance

One possible explanation involves the safety of the screen. Watching a pimple being squeezed puts you close enough to see everything without any chance of its contents reaching you.

Wabnegger compares this with enjoying a horror film: an uncomfortable experience can become entertaining when the viewer feels safe.

His later research has also linked pimple-popping enjoyment with morbid curiosity, an interest in disturbing or threatening subjects. That association offers a possible clue to the appeal, rather than establishing why any individual watches.

Some viewers say the videos help them relax. Wabnegger wants to investigate what prompts people to seek them out and how they feel afterwards. Whether watching helps people sleep remains untested.

Listen to the episode for the science behind this divisive viewing habit, and my increasingly unsubtle attempts to secure a place in his next experiment.

Have you spotted a bizarre health trend you’d like us to investigate? Email strangehealth@theconversation.com. The stranger the question, the better.

Strange Health is hosted by Katie Edwards and Dan Baumgardt. The executive producer is Gemma Ware, with editing and mixing by Anouk Millet. Artwork by Alice Mason.

Listen to Strange Health on your preferred podcast app, download it via our RSS feed or find out how else to listen here.

articles.title: Brain lesions: what causes them and when they need follow-up
articles.summary:
Brain scans can help doctors identify lesions, which are areas of damaged or abnormal tissue. Gorodenkoff/Shutterstock

You open your brain scan report and see the word “lesion”. It’s a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor.

In a report, it means there’s an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that’s been there for years.

What happens next depends on what the radiologist thinks they’re looking at.

Take a stroke. If a clot blocks an artery supplying the brain, the tissue downstream is starved of oxygen. Brain cells can die, leaving an area of damage that doctors call an infarct. Even a tiny stroke in an area that controls movement can leave someone with lasting weakness. If your face suddenly droops on one side or you develop arm weakness or trouble speaking, call 999 straight away, even if the symptoms pass.

A lesion can also form through inflammation. In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibres. Damage to that coating makes it harder for messages to travel along the nerves. The damaged areas can show up on MRI scans in the brain or spinal cord. Doctors look at where those areas are and what pattern they form, because several other conditions can produce spots on an MRI.

Sometimes the lesion is a growth. A meningioma is a tumour that starts in the protective layers of tissue around the brain. Most meningiomas are non-cancerous and grow slowly. They can go unnoticed for years and turn up on a scan that’s being carried out for another reason. Even a non-cancerous tumour can cause symptoms if it presses on the brain.

What the scan can tell you about a lesion

If you’ve ever looked at a set of MRI images, you might have noticed that the fluid around the brain can look bright in one picture and dark in another. Think of how an Instagram filter makes some details stand out. The MRI scanner does something similar by changing how it captures the image.

Radiologists call these different settings “sequences”. One can turn down the signal from the fluid so that patches of abnormal tissue next to it stand out. Another is sensitive to the movement of water within tissue and can help pick up a recent stroke.

Comparing brain scans taken at different times can help doctors see whether a lesion has changed.
PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Sometimes the radiologist will go looking for an older scan. If the same area looked exactly the same several years ago, that gives them information a single scan can’t. If there’s no earlier scan to compare it with, a repeat scan may help show whether the lesion is changing over time.

When a brain lesion needs follow-up

Some findings on a scan can be left alone. An arachnoid cyst is a pocket of fluid in one of the membranes around the brain. On a scan, it typically has a clear outline, and the fluid inside looks the same as the fluid that normally surrounds the brain. In adults, a small cyst with these features often needs no further scans if it causes no symptoms and is in a place where it’s unlikely to block the flow of fluid.

For some lesions, a repeat scan helps doctors see whether they’re growing. If a meningioma is found by chance and is causing no symptoms, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence suggests a repeat scan after a year. If the tumour looks the same, clinicians can consider ending follow-up or scanning again five years after it was first found.

If the scan shows a brain abscess, a pocket of pus in the brain caused by an infection, the next step is urgent treatment in hospital.

If you’re reading your own report, look for the summary, often headed “impression” or “conclusion”. That’s where the radiologist usually gives their best explanation of what they’ve seen and may suggest a next step. When you speak to the clinician who arranged the scan, ask what they think caused the lesion and whether you need to do anything about it. If they recommend another scan, ask what they’ll be looking for.

articles.title: From novels to GTA 6: the long history of fears about addictive entertainment
articles.summary:
The release of Grand Theft Auto VI has renewed concerns about excessive gaming, but spending hours immersed in a video game does not necessarily indicate addiction. SolidMaks/Shutterstock

The release of Grand Theft Auto VI, arguably the most anticipated video game in history, has prompted warnings about excessive gaming. Addiction specialists have urged players to recognise when gaming begins to interfere with their lives, while experts have raised concerns about its potential effects on younger players. These warnings reflect broader concerns about gaming addiction, rather than evidence that GTA VI itself is particularly addictive.

There are genuine health concerns behind these fears. The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition wherein someone loses control over their gaming, prioritising it to the extent that there are serious consequences.

Taking a sneaky sick day for a marathon gaming session when a new game launches isn’t the issue. Gaming disorder is far more serious. It involves significant disruption to someone’s personal life, relationships, education or work.

Gaming disorder is a recognised health condition, and researchers have investigated how common it is. But the broader fear that people might become so absorbed in fictional worlds that they neglect everyday life predates video games. Similar concerns were once directed at other forms of entertainment, including novels.

Fiction fixation

As novels became increasingly popular during the eighteenth century, they attracted the same criticism that video games receive today. In Germany, commentators coined the term “Lesesucht”, meaning “reading addiction” or “reading mania”, to describe what they saw as an unhealthy obsession with books.

In England, critics worried that people would spend too much time reading novels and struggle to distinguish fiction from reality. Young women were considered particularly vulnerable, with fears that romantic stories might corrupt their morals or encourage unrealistic expectations about what they might expect from life.

Prominent writers joined the debate. In his autobiography Biographia Literaria, the poet and critic Samuel Taylor Coleridge criticised readers of popular fiction for losing themselves in daydreams rather than thinking critically about what they read. Jane Austen, meanwhile, defended novels as a serious form of literature in Northanger Abbey.

The fears continued as new forms of entertainment emerged. During the 19th century, cheap adventure and crime stories known as penny dreadfuls in Britain and dime novels in America were blamed for encouraging juvenile crime.

In 1954, following growing concerns about the influence of horror and crime comics on children, the American comics industry established the Comics Code Authority, which imposed restrictions on what publishers could show.

Later, critics accused television of turning audiences into passive viewers and taking time away from more worthwhile activities, including reading. More recently, streaming services and binge-watching have revived concerns about spending too much time absorbed in entertainment.

Although the form of entertainment changes, the underlying fear remains familiar: that popular stories can have a harmful influence on the people who enjoy them.

Novels and video games share an important attraction. Both can transport us into fictional worlds, allowing us to escape everyday life, explore unfamiliar experiences and become emotionally involved in stories.

Moral panics

Many historical fears about popular entertainment reflected the social attitudes and prejudices of their time. But fiction can influence how people see themselves and the world around them. It can shape expectations, encourage dissatisfaction with everyday life or offer an escape from problems that people would rather avoid.

Video games can be particularly absorbing because they allow players to take an active part in fictional worlds. Instead of simply following a story, players can explore, make decisions and influence what happens.

Some games also encourage people to keep playing by regularly introducing new challenges, rewards and items to collect. In Grand Theft Auto Online, the online version of GTA V, new vehicles and weapons were continually released, giving players reasons to return and avoid missing out.

This approach can also encourage spending. Players can use real money to purchase in-game currency, which can then be spent on virtual items. Such features have helped make the franchise enormously profitable, with GTA V and its online component reportedly generating an estimated US$10 billion in revenue since the game’s release in 2013.

These commercial strategies raise important questions about how games are designed to keep people playing and spending money. For those already struggling to control their gaming, systems that offer frequent rewards and encourage repeated play may be particularly concerning.

However, gaming disorder affects a relatively small minority of people. A review of research from 17 countries estimated that around 2% of the general population experiences gaming disorder, although estimates varied considerably between studies.

Spending a lot of time playing video games does not, by itself, mean someone has an addiction. What matters is whether they have lost control over their gaming and whether it is causing serious problems in their everyday life.

Gaming can provide an escape from difficult circumstances, just as books, television and other forms of entertainment can. The reasons someone plays, and the effects gaming has on their life, are therefore more revealing than the number of hours they spend doing it.

So, if you or someone you know is currently spending a lot of time in Vice City, you probably needn’t worry. We shouldn’t judge someone’s gaming habits simply by counting the hours they play, any more than we would judge their reading habits by counting the pages they finish.

Someone pretending to have a cold to get a day off work for a new game’s release may simply be enjoying a rare occasion. But if they repeatedly miss work, neglect relationships or struggle to stop playing despite serious consequences, there may be cause for concern.

James O'Sullivan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Nearly half of autistic girls are persistently absent from secondary school – new research
articles.summary:
Ben Molyneux/Shutterstock

Children not attending school has become a growing national concern in England. Government policy has increasingly focused on improving attendance, while parents can face fines for unauthorised absences.

However, behind this wider attendance problem is a striking disparity. Our recently published research shows that between 2021 and 2023, nearly half (44%) of autistic girls attending mainstream secondary schools in England were persistently absent, meaning they miss 10% or more of school.

This high level of absence is not seen equally across all pupils. In 2022-23, 31% of autistic boys in mainstream secondary schools were persistently absent, compared with around 25% of girls and 20% of boys with no identified special educational need. Although absence has increased significantly across all groups since the pandemic, autistic girls stand out as being particularly likely to miss significant amounts of school.

Before the pandemic, around 25% of autistic girls in secondary schools were persistently absent. By 2021-22, this had risen to 44% and remained at a similar level in 2022-23. Although absence increased for all pupils over this period, the gap between autistic girls and autistic boys widened considerably – absence in boys rose from 18% to 31%.

Importantly, there are signs that difficulties with attendance may begin much earlier in a child’s life following the pandemic. In 2022-23, 28% of autistic girls in primary school were persistently absent, compared with 26.5% of autistic boys. Before the pandemic, in 2018-19, 16.6% of primary-aged autistic girls and 15% of autistic boys were persistently absent.

Although the difference between autistic girls and boys is much smaller in primary school than in secondary school, these findings suggest that we need to start paying closer attention to attendance difficulties earlier.

Finding the data

Despite the scale of these differences, it has been difficult to tease out using publicly available school attendance data. Government figures have routinely grouped children with different types of special educational need together, masking the scale of the attendance problem for autistic girls within the wider statistics.

To better understand attendance figures for autistic girls specifically, we used a freedom of information request to obtain national attendance data from the Department for Education, broken down by autism, sex, and school stage. This allowed us to examine attendance patterns across 5 to 6 million pupils in state-funded schools in England each year, and compare attendance for autistic girls, autistic boys, and girls and boys with no identified special educational need.

Rates of absence from primary school have also increased.
Rawpixel.com/Shutterstock

These figures, however, only tell us part of the story. They show how many autistic girls are missing significant amounts of school, but they cannot tell us why this is the case, or what might be making school increasingly difficult to attend.

We know from our previous research with autistic children and families that difficulties with school can build up over time. Autistic young people describe sensory and social pressures, difficult relationships with school staff and school environments that do not always understand or respond to their needs. Over time, these experiences can make school increasingly difficult to manage, and can affect whether young people feel safe, supported, and that they belong.

Our ongoing, as yet unpublished wider research with autistic girls and their families has demonstrated that, for many, difficulties with school attendance stemmed not from a lack of motivation to attend or learn, but from their experiences at school and the associated emotional impact. One girl explained to us that teachers “just thought I was just another kid who wanted to bunk lessons and didn’t want to go to them, but it wasn’t the case. Like I wanted to go to lessons. I wanted to get an education”.

Attending school might be more challenging as children transition to secondary school. Pupils must manage bigger and busier environments, different subject teachers and classrooms, changing friendships and larger academic and organisational demands.

For autistic girls who may already be struggling and hiding their difficulties to fit in, it may not always be obvious to others how difficult they are finding school. By the time attendance starts to become a serious concern, the difficulties affecting their attendance may already have been building up over months or years.

Hanna Kovshoff has received funding from the British Academy/Leverhulme.

Chloe Eddy receives PhD funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

Sarah Parsons receives funding from the British Academy / Leverhulme.

articles.title: The curious history of the huntaway, New Zealand’s unusually loud sheepdog
articles.summary:
The New Zealand Huntaway sheepdog. Tonia Kraakman/Shutterstock

Sheepdog trials don’t always take place in a field. Some take place in a pub.

Across New Zealand, “bark-ups” are a common sight at pubs and agricultural events, and feature a home-bred invention: the New Zealand huntaway dog breed. The aim of the bark-up is simple: find the dog with the best bark.

To outsiders, the spectacle raises an obvious question: why would anyone hold a competition to find the sheepdog that barks the loudest? The answer lies not just in the sheep stations of New Zealand where the huntaway was developed, but in the colonisation of New Zealand, for sheepdogs are breeds of empire. It’s something I explore in my new book.

The modern sheepdog was a Victorian invention. Queen Victoria herself was a fan of the collie, buying the best from shepherds on the England-Scotland borders. Those shepherds were at the helm of the emerging sheepdog trialling scene at the start of the 20th century.

In the process, sheepdogs came to embody Victorian moral values. The ideal dog displayed discipline, intelligence, restraint, obedience and industriousness, and perhaps most of all, silence while working – qualities that were equally applicable to the shepherd.

Organisations such as the International Sheep Dog Society reinforced these ideals. Under its influential honorary secretary, James Reid, the border collie was invented not merely as a useful farm dog but as the pinnacle of canine improvement.

Exported throughout Britain’s settler colonies, it became a breed of empire, carrying with it particular ideas about good stockmanship, moral character and agricultural modernity. Reid went so far as to describe the sheepdog as the foundation of the pastoral economy, whose intelligence and labour underpinned the success of the British empire.

Scottish settlers had already taken their sheepdogs to New Zealand in the mid-19th Century. But it would be a Northumbrian, James Lilico, who would transform New Zealand’s sheepdogs. Arriving in 1894 to work as a shepherd, he immediately sent home for his dog Captain, disappointed by the “useless mongrels” he had been given to work.

So started half a century of importing the finest sheepdogs he could source, usually championship winning trial dogs, earning him the title of the “collie king of New Zealand”. Lilico imported sheepdogs that had been bred with the quality known as “eye” (herding using an intense stare) that had become highly valued among triallists. Breeding them, Lilico championed the superiority of what he called “border dogs” in his weekly column in the New Zealand Farmer periodical.

Lilico’s actions were not universally welcomed, in particular his criticism of the sheepdogs and shepherds who worked New Zealand’s high country. For the shepherds of these regions, Lilico’s strong-eyed dogs were too slow, too delicate and insufficiently forceful. In their view, sheep needed to be moved, not mesmerised.

Their alternative was the huntaway. What marked out the huntaway from the border collie was its noise. Without fences and across wide open country, noise had become a valuable tool for shepherds. Before setting out to muster sheep, shepherds gathered their dogs and instructed them to bark. This bark up – just like those now seen in pubs – guided sheep from a distance, so by the time shepherds arrived the sheep were already on the move.

Read more:
Your dog may be wilder than you think, according to canine sleep research

If its bark united the huntaway, their appearance did anything but. Old photographs reveal a variety of different appearances and types: from small and fluffy to larger looking collies. But as sheep farming expanded from the South Island into the hill country of the North Island, the huntaway began to evolve.

To make the huntaway more powerful to deal with stubborn Romney sheep, its voice got louder. Breeding experiments involving mastiff, rottweiler, labrador, hound and other breeds sought to improve its barking power. A bigger huntaway became more common, but even now the huntaway defies standardisation beyond its capacity to bark all day.

Crucially, while the development of New Zealand agriculture was part of a scientific “grasslands revolution”, these scientists had little to do with sheepdogs. The huntaway instead reflected the spirit of farmers, as a “practical dog for practical men”. Scientists and breed societies were kept well away in fear of ruining the dog.

The Huntaway.

Recognition and uncertainty

In 2013 the huntaway was recognised as a unique breed by the New Zealand Kennel Club, but its origins were still uncertain. Recent genetic studies show that it is related to the border collie, and other breeds imported in the 19th century. Genetic traces of the breeds used for power are harder to find, reinforcing the mythology that surrounds the breed.

It may also be that its defining feature – the bark – is not simply a New Zealand invention but an echo of its past. Back in Scotland in 1935, James Reid had given a lecture celebrating the border collie conquering all other breeds of sheepdog. Its popularity had meant that other barking sheepdogs used across Wales and southern England had no place, consigning them to history.

When James Lilico wrote about the huntaway in one of his three books, he received a letter from a shepherd in north Wales suggesting that the Huntaway sounded no different to the dog known as ci hanos, a dog that used noise to drive sheep onto the hills in the springtime.

Lilico had planned on importing one of these as part of a breeding experiment. Such an experiment might be more valuable today as the huntaway gene pool narrows: the closure of large sheep stations in New Zealand is making breeding selection a challenge. In doing so, it raises existential questions about sheepdogs themselves, because without sheep there will be no sheepdogs.
